articles.title: Moving diagnostics upstream: prehospital blood gas analysis is associated with safe community care and improved patient selection for hospital admission.
Association of caregiver burden with the healthcare use and outcomes of older patients attending the ED.
Social Risk Screening and Referrals in the Pediatric Inpatient Setting.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Many professional organizations recently recommended inpatient screening for social risks. Although prior studies have explored social risk screening rates in children's hospitals, many excluded community hospitals and lacked detail on screening practices. We aimed to describe national social risk screening and referral practices among hospitals caring for children.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a cross-sectional survey (August 2023-November 2023) through the Pediatric Research in Inpatient Settings Network. One clinical leader per institution was surveyed on inpatient social risk screening and referral processes, populations, tools and data tracking, and barriers/facilitators to social care. Descriptive statistics summarized survey responses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the hospitals contacted, 80.2% (77/96) completed the survey. Overall, 66.7% of hospitals reported screening for social risks in some capacity, most commonly performed by nurses. Screening tools and domains varied widely, with 21.9% using a published tool and 12.5% using internally developed questions. Food insecurity was the most frequently screened domain (91.9%), whereas screening for legal needs was least common (0%). Most hospitals had systems to refer patients to in-hospital (98.4%) and out-of-hospital (96.8%) services, primarily through social work consultations (96.5%) and printed handouts (54.4%). Fewer than 10% partnered with community-based organizations. Less than 45% of screening hospitals had a data-tracking system for referrals, and only 2.5% collected patient health care use data. Staffing was the most cited barrier to screening.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Social risk screening and referral practices vary widely among hospitals caring for children. Standardized policies and support mechanisms may reduce variability and promote equitable social care practices across hospitals.

articles.title: Association of Early Primary Care Follow-Up With Acute Care Use After ICU Discharge.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To determine if early primary care follow-up after pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) hospitalization is associated with reduced acute care use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using claims data from publicly and privately insured children, we identified a cohort of PICU hospitalizations from January 2016 to December 2019. We matched children with and without early primary care follow-up (within 7 days of hospital discharge) 1 to 1 on demographic and clinical characteristics. We compared the number of days of acute care use (emergency department or rehospitalization) during days 8 to 90 postdischarge using negative binomial regression and reported incidence rate ratios (IRR).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The sample included 180 516 PICU hospitalizations, including 158 544 for publicly insured children and 21 972 for privately insured children. Among PICU hospitalizations for publicly and privately insured children, 56 247 (35.4%) and 5156 (23.5%) were associated with acute care use with 8 to 90 days postdischarge. Hospitalizations of children with early primary care follow-up were less likely to be associated with acute care use than those without follow-up (public insurance: IRR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96; P < .001; and private insurance: IRR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.63-0.77; P < .001). Subgroup analyses suggested early primary care follow-up was associated with larger decreases in acute care after hospitalizations of older children and children with sepsis. The association between early primary care follow-up and acute care use persisted in a secondary analysis using data from 2022 to 2023.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Early primary care follow-up was associated with lower acute care use after discharge from PICU hospitalization. Promotion of early primary care follow-up may be warranted after pediatric critical illness.

articles.title: Optimizing Antibiotic Duration for Pneumonia and Sinusitis in the Pediatric Emergency Department.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Updates to national and international guidelines now recommend shortening antibiotic durations to 3 to 5 days for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and 5 to 7 days for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS). We aimed to increase the percentage of children discharged home from the emergency department with CAP or ABRS who were treated with an optimal antibiotic duration from 13% to 70% by July 2025.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We assembled a multidisciplinary team and used quality improvement tools, including cause-and-effect analysis, driver diagram, and prioritization matrix, to identify impactful interventions. We also surveyed prescriber comfort with shorter antibiotic durations. Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles included implementing new clinical pathways (CP), electronic health record (EHR) updates, and educating prescribers. Our outcome metric was the percentage of patients receiving recommended antibiotic duration for CAP and ABRS. Process metrics included use of CP Quick Response codes and CAP "Quick-Discharge" order sets. Balancing metric was the number of return visits with the same diagnosis within 14 days.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We saw shifts in the outcome metric center line in August 2023, February 2024, and November 2024 from 13.1% to 64.8%. These changes primarily reflected CAP duration because it was the more common diagnosis, although ABRS short antibiotic durations showed similar improvement during this time frame. Process metrics showed an increase over time. There was no change in balancing metric.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: We significantly improved antibiotic prescription durations for CAP and ABRS through CP changes, EHR updates, prescriber education and feedback, and resource distribution.

articles.title: Long-term health, criminal justice, and socioeconomic outcomes among people subject to compulsory mental health care in Norway: a nationwide registry cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Compulsory mental health care aims to manage risk and treatment needs among people with severe mental illness, but evidence on long-term outcomes across health, justice, and socioeconomic domains is scarce. We aimed to compare long-term outcomes across adult groups defined by community treatment orders (CTOs), compulsory hospitalisation, compulsory observation, and voluntary mental health care, and the general population.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this nationwide registry cohort study, we identified all individuals aged 18-65 years with specialist mental health-care contact in Norway from Jan 1, 2015, to Dec 31, 2016 and general population comparators sampled via Statistics Norway based on age and sex. Follow-up was through 2021-23, depending on registry availability. Study groups were defined hierarchically: CTO, compulsory hospitalisation without CTO, compulsory observation without compulsory hospitalisation or CTO, voluntary mental health care, and no specialist mental health-care contact (ie, the general population). Outcomes included mortality and cause of death, self-harm treated in emergency departments or hospital, substance use disorder, victimisation, violent or sexual offence charges or imprisonment, subsequent compulsory care, acute admissions, and socioeconomic outcomes. Data for all groups were sourced from linked nationwide registries. Separate binomial regressions estimated sex-specific probabilities by group, adjusting for birth year. People with lived experience of mental health services advised study design and interpretation.

abstract.label: FINDINGS
abstract.text: The final study sample comprised 321 708 individuals (mean age 36·5 years, range 18-65) across five mutually exclusive groups: CTO (n=3331), compulsory hospitalisation (n=2907), compulsory observation (n=2554), voluntary care (n=177 396), and general population (n=135 520), 193 473 (60·1%) were female and 128 235 (39·9%) were male; ethnicity data were unavailable. Compulsory care groups were associated with substantially worse long-term outcomes across health, criminal justice, and socioeconomic domains than voluntary patients and the general population. Across compulsory care groups, female participants had higher adjusted probabilities of self-harm or suicide than male participants, whereas male participants had higher adjusted probabilities of substance use disorder and of being charged with or imprisoned for violent or sexual offences compared with female participants. The compulsory observation group had the highest adjusted probabilities of self-harm or suicide and substance use disorder across the five groups. Self-harm or suicide was recorded in 135 (12·1%) of 1115 female participants (adjusted probability 12% [95% CI 10-14]) and 75 (5·7%) of 1308 male participants (5·5% [4·4-6·9]). Substance use disorder was recorded in 407 (39·1%) of 1041 female participants (39% [36-42]) and 639 (53·2%) of 1202 male participants (53% [50-56]). Charges or imprisonment for violent or sexual offences were recorded in 146 (14·2%) of 1030 female participants (14% [12-16]) and 446 (37·4% [34-40]) of 1194 male participants. During 2015-21, including the inclusion period, suicide and other external causes accounted for 132 (55·7%) of 237 classified deaths in compulsory observation, compared with 1818 (38·2%) of 4754 in voluntary care and 174 (18·6%) of 938 in the general population. The CTO group had the highest adjusted probability of disability benefit receipt: 89% (95% CI 87-91) in female participants and 93% (92-94) in male participants; a substantial minority of disability-benefit recipients in the CTO group also had earned income.

abstract.label: INTERPRETATION
abstract.text: Compulsory care groups were associated with distinct long-term prognoses from the voluntary care and general population groups. These findings provide population-level benchmarks for service planning and policy evaluation and show that legally defined compulsory care groups should not be treated as a single prognostic population.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: Research Council of Norway.

articles.title: Vestibular Event Monitoring in the Community and Emergency Room.

abstract.text: Patients who are experiencing an attack of acute vertigo often demonstrate nystagmus that could provide useful diagnostic clues that identify the underlying vestibular disorder. Such ictal nystagmus is encountered in primary care, emergency rooms and patients' home environments where methods of recording nystagmus (video nystagmography) are scarce. Investigators worldwide have endeavored to circumvent this difficulty by using novel service models or portable nystagmus recording devices. Here we describe the event-monitoring techniques used thus far and summarize the diagnostic information gathered by ictal video nystagmography.

articles.title: Prehospital Care of Older Adults Following Perceived Low-Acuity Falls and Related "Lift Assist" Encounters: An NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document.

abstract.text: Older adults who present as low-acuity falls requiring mobilization assistance, commonly referred to as a "lift assist", represent a common reason for EMS activation. These encounters often involve underlying medical conditions or injuries that are not immediately apparent, and missed or delayed diagnosis is associated with adverse outcomes. At the same time, some patients are transported to the emergency department when it is not necessary, exposing them to potential harms and contributing to increased health care utilization. These encounters are therefore complex clinical presentations and represent important opportunities for thorough assessment and higher-order clinical decision making, supported by systems that enable appropriate disposition and follow-up. However, there is a system-level bias, beginning in initial education and reinforced through dispatch, policy, and protocol, that frames these encounters as uniformly low-acuity, non-medical, minor traumas leading to underassessment and limiting clinical decision-making. Therefore, NAEMSP recommends:EMS systems should recognize calls for falls or "lift assists" as patient encounters that warrant an assessment, including evaluation for underlying medical causes, traumatic injuries, and safety, and frame these encounters as opportunities for higher-order clinical decision-making within the broader context of geriatric syndromes rather than isolated low-acuity events.EMS systems should support transport decisions based on a thorough assessment and patient-centered discussion, recognizing that not all patients require ED transport and that safe alternatives may include non-transport or referral to appropriate follow-up pathways.EMS systems should track the assessment of patients encountered during "lift assist" responses and older adults following perceived low acuity falls as a system-level quality measure to monitor performance and drive improvement.Policymakers and payers should implement sustainable reimbursement structures that support EMS assessment and care even when transport does not occur.

articles.title: The Effect of Psychiatric Medication Use on 1- to 3-Level Elective Lumbar Fusion Outcomes.

abstract.label: OUTCOMES
abstract.text: The impact of psychiatric medication use, particularly antipsychotics, on lumbar fusion outcomes remains poorly defined. This study evaluated peri- and postoperative outcomes following 1- to 3-level lumbar fusion among patients using antidepressants or antipsychotics.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a single-center, retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent 1- to 3-level lumbar fusion between 2022 and 2025 at a large, academic, inner-city tertiary care hospital. Data extracted from the electronic medical record included demographic information, insurance status, Charlson Comorbidity Index, psychiatric medication use, intraoperative variables, perioperative complications, and discharge disposition. Postoperative outcomes included 90-day reoperation, readmission, emergency department visits, revision surgery, persistent radicular pain, and continued opioid use at maximum follow-up. Patients were divided into an antidepressant group (current antidepressant use with no antipsychotic use) and an antipsychotic group (current antipsychotic use regardless of antidepressant use) based on medication utilization at the time of surgery. Both treatment groups were subsequently compared with a control group (no active psychiatric medication use) using univariate and multivariate regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 615 patients, 75.6% took no psychiatric medications, 19.8% took antidepressants, and 4.6% took antipsychotics. Patients taking psychiatric medications were more likely to be women (P = 0.02) with otherwise similar baseline characteristics. On univariate analysis, both antidepressant and antipsychotic use were associated with higher revision rates (8.2% vs 3.0%, P = 0.01; 17.9% vs 3.0%, P < 0.001). Antidepressant use was also associated with increased 90-day emergency department visits (P = 0.029), readmissions (P = 0.029), and persistent opioid use (P = 0.01). In multivariate analysis, antidepressant (OR: 2.74, 95% CI: 1.177-6.398) and antipsychotic use (OR: 5.99, 95% CI: 1.954-18.362) were independently associated with revision surgery, while antidepressant use was also associated with persistent opioid use (OR: 2.07, 95% CI: 1.163-3.684).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Antidepressant and antipsychotic use were independently associated with increased odds of revision surgery following lumbar fusion. Additional studies are required to understand class-specific effects and underlying mechanisms.

abstract.label: CLINICAL RELEVANCE
abstract.text: The association between preoperative psychiatric medication use with poor postoperative outcomes highlights the need for further investigation into psychiatric comorbidity and clinical outcomes in spine surgery LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 3.

articles.title: Association between the site of emergency care and patient-centered outcomes in patients with cancer: rationale and design of the French COVER cohort.
articles.journal_full: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine

abstract.text: Patients living with cancer now account for a substantial and growing share of emergency department (ED) visits and carry a high burden of hospitalization and in-hospital death. Their acute presentations are frequently multifactorial - driven by disease progression, treatment toxicity, immunosuppression, or the decompensation of comorbid conditions. They may present with higher rates of complications because of novel therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors and cellular therapies, whose emergency manifestations remain unfamiliar to many emergency physicians. Despite this growing importance, the unscheduled care of patients with cancer has received comparatively little dedicated research. How these patients are managed in the ED, how often the emergency physician can access the oncology medical record and goals of care, how the acute complications of new anticancer therapies present, and how a background of cancer should modify the diagnostic approach to everyday emergencies remain poorly characterized. To address these gaps, the Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment was designed as a prospective, multicenter French cohort of consecutive adults with active cancer or in remission for less than 1 year, presenting to the ED for any reason. Enrollment took place across a national network of 76 EDs for two 1-week periods (summer 2025 and winter 2025-2026), with follow-up to 90 days, yielding a large sample of patients designed as a platform for multiple analyses. The primary aim of Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment is to determine whether being managed in an ED located within the patient's own cancer referral center, rather than any other hospital, is associated with improvement in morbidity and mortality, captured by the number of days alive and out of hospital at 30 days. Beyond this primary aim, the cohort will support a broad research program on the place of the ED in the cancer care pathway, from patient profiling and pathway description to the emergency toxicities of anticancer drugs and the cancer-specific features of common presentations.

articles.title: Epidemiology, clinical profile, and outcomes of older patients with active cancer attending at Spanish emergency departments (EDEN-56 study).
articles.journal_full: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Older adults with active cancer are increasing, clinically complex emergency department (ED) population, but large multicenter European data are limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe the epidemiology, baseline characteristics, diagnoses, and outcomes of older patients with active cancer attending Spanish EDs, and assess whether associations between active cancer and short-term outcomes varied with age and sex.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Secondary analysis of the Emergency Department and Elder Needs retrospective multicenter registry, including all patients aged greater than or equal to 65 years attending 52 Spanish EDs during 1-7 April 2019. Patients with and without active cancer were compared. Annualized incidence was extrapolated overall, by sex, and by age. Age-related patterns were modeled using restricted cubic splines.

abstract.label: OUTCOME AND ANALYSIS
abstract.text: ED length of stay, hospitalization, length of hospitalization, and index-episode death. Age-by-cancer and age-by-sex interactions were assessed in unadjusted and multivariable models.

abstract.label: MAIN RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 25 557 older ED patients, 4701 (18.4%) had active cancer. The estimated annualized incidence of ED presentations was 10 885 per 100 000 inhabitants aged greater than or equal to 65 years [95% confidence interval (CI): 10 576-11 200], higher in men (annualized rate ratio: 1.80, 95% CI: 1.70-1.91) and in the mid-to-late 80s. Patients with cancer had more severe comorbidity (58.9 vs. 12.9%), polypharmacy (26.6 vs. 21.3%), and walking handicaps (31.5 vs. 28.2%). Malignancy accounted for only 7.7% of ED diagnoses in the cancer group; infections, heart failure, and respiratory conditions were frequent. Active cancer was associated with longer median ED stay (4.0 vs. 3.3 h; adjusted difference: 0.3, 95% CI: 0.1-0.4), higher hospitalization [32.5 vs. 24.0%; adjusted odds ratio (OR): 1.34, 95% CI: 1.25-1.44], longer median hospitalization (7.5 vs. 6.9 days; adjusted difference: 0.5, 0.1-0.9), and higher index-episode mortality (5.5 vs. 2.5%; adjusted OR: 2.12, 95% CI: 1.81-2.50). Age significantly modified ED length of stay, hospitalization, and mortality, with significantly different age-related changes between patients with and without cancer. Among patients with cancer, age-related trajectories did not significantly differ by sex.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Active cancer is common among older ED patients and associated with substantial resource use and worse short-term outcomes. These associations vary with age, supporting multidimensional assessment beyond chronological age or cancer status alone.

articles.title: A Miniaturized, Multilayer Structured Vertical Flow Paper Device Enabled One-Step, Multiplex, Spontaneous Detection of Biomarkers in Microliter Blood for Disease Screening.

abstract.text: Developing a miniaturized, portable device for multiplexed detection of a library of protein biomarkers from microliter blood sample is critical for early disease screening in many scenarios, such as home healthcare and emergency care. However, major challenges remain, including multiplexed detection without cross-interference, system-level miniaturization, reliable flow manipulation, and simple user operation. Here, we present a miniaturized, multilayer structured vertical flow paper device that enables one-step, multiplexed, spontaneous detection of biomarkers in microliter blood for screening of heart disease, kidney disease, and inflammation. The device is designed with a multilayer membrane structure that integrates 3D-printed glass fiber membranes, wax-printed nitrocellulose membranes, and cellulose absorption membranes, enabling autonomous wicking of the sample through the device while concurrently distributing the sample into multiple equal parts and executing the sandwich immunoassay and washing steps. Simultaneous quantification of 12 biomarkers is achieved, and clinical performance is validated using clinical samples from patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), acute kidney disease (AKD), or sepsis. The device requires about 60 μL of sample, delivers results in 15 min, and is also compact (12.5 cm3). Overall, this platform provides a novel and universal strategy for miniaturized multiplexed immunoassays for rapid clinical screening.

articles.title: Prehospital Risk Stratification for Early Transfusion in Pediatric Trauma: A National Trauma Data Bank Analysis.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Pediatric criteria remain limited for identifying injured children who may benefit from early blood transfusion for hemorrhagic shock. This study evaluated whether emergency medical services (EMS)-observable variables in a national trauma registry could identify children at risk for early hospital blood transfusion.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study using the National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2020). Among 391,126 records for patients aged 1-15 years, we included children transported by EMS directly from the scene to a participating trauma center after excluding burn injuries, interfacility transfers, and missing pre-identified EMS variables (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, or Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS]). The primary outcome was any blood product administered within 4 h of emergency department arrival. Five prespecified EMS-observable predictors composed the model: age-adjusted hypotension, age-adjusted tachycardia, GCS ≤ 14, penetrating mechanism, and prehospital traumatic cardiac arrest. We fit a multivariable logistic regression and a classification and regression tree (CART) using an 80/20 stratified train-validation split. Missing data sensitivity analyses included multiple imputation and CART refitting in the broader eligible cohort.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 79,764 children, 2,634 (3.3%) received early transfusion in the hospital. All five predictors were independently associated with early transfusion, led by GCS ≤ 14 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.38; 95% confidence interval [CI], 7.61-9.22), penetrating mechanism (aOR 5.87; 95% CI, 5.28-6.51), and age-adjusted hypotension (aOR 5.39; 95% CI, 4.74-6.13). In the validation cohort, CART analysis stratified patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk tiers comprising 77.0%, 19.7%, and 3.3% of patients, respectively. Early-transfusion rates were 1.2%, 6.1%, and 36.7% across these tiers. The high-risk tier accounted for 36.8% of all early transfusion events. Using the high-risk tier as a decision threshold, sensitivity was 36.8%, specificity 97.8%, positive predictive value 36.7%, and negative predictive value 97.8%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Five EMS-observable features, including age-adjusted hypotension, age-adjusted tachycardia, GCS ≤ 14, penetrating mechanism, and prehospital traumatic cardiac arrest, identified a small subgroup of pediatric trauma patients with substantially elevated risk of early hospital transfusion. This parsimonious framework may inform prospective validation of prehospital transfusion criteria.

articles.title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery.

abstract.label: DESCRIPTION
abstract.text: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion.

abstract.label: ALTERNATIVES
abstract.text: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8.

abstract.label: RATIONALE
abstract.text: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport.

abstract.label: EXPECTED OUTCOMES
abstract.text: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence.

abstract.label: IMPORTANT TIPS
abstract.text: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics.

abstract.label: ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS
abstract.text: RICE = rest, ice, compression, elevationMRI = magnetic resonance imagingBID = twice daily.

articles.title: Twenty-five years of the NIDA clinical trials network and the future of addiction research.
articles.journal_full: Journal of substance use and addiction treatment

abstract.text: The National Institute on Drug Abuse Clinical Trials Network (CTN) was established in 1999 to bridge the persistent divide between addiction research and clinical practice through partnerships between researchers and community treatment providers. This editorial examines the evolution of the CTN over its first 25 years and considers priorities for its future. Drawing on the historical development of the Network and articles in this 25-year special collection, we examine changes in the populations and settings represented in CTN research, the incorporation of implementation science, the evolution of community partnerships, the scientific value of accumulated CTN data and experience, and emerging clinical and methodological priorities. Over 25 years, the CTN has developed from a network focused principally on clinically relevant effectiveness trials into a broader national infrastructure for clinical trials and translational addiction research. Its research has expanded beyond specialty addiction treatment programs into primary care, emergency departments, hospitals, community health centers, pharmacies, and other settings in which people with substance use disorders receive care. The Network has also increasingly addressed populations historically underrepresented in addiction research, incorporated implementation questions into clinical research, strengthened community engagement, and used accumulated trial data and emerging analytic methods to generate new scientific knowledge. These developments demonstrate that the value of a clinical research network extends beyond individual trial outcomes. Clinical trials should remain at the core of the CTN's scientific mission. However, trial designs and complementary research methods should be determined by the scientific questions being addressed. The CTN's future impact will depend on its ability to conduct rigorous multisite trials while incorporating implementation, representation, community partnership, and accumulated data and responding rapidly to changes in the drug supply and addiction care environment. These capabilities can help the Network generate evidence that is rigorous, relevant, timely, and more likely to improve addiction care.

articles.title: Diagnostic Yield of Neuroimaging in Patients With Nonindex Seizures in the Emergency Department.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: The diagnostic yield of neuroimaging in patients with nonindex seizures, defined as those with established epilepsy presenting to the emergency department with a recurrent seizure, remains uncertain. Although head computed tomography (CT) is frequently performed, its impact on clinical decision-making is often limited. This study aimed to assess the frequency of neuroimaging use, its diagnostic yield, and the clinical factors associated with acute findings leading to management changes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients with epilepsy presenting with nonindex seizures to a tertiary public hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, between February 2023 and February 2024. Sociodemographic, clinical, and neuroimaging data were extracted from electronic medical records. Descriptive and bivariate analyses were performed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 307 patients were included (median age: 39 y; 58.6% male). Head CT was performed in 79.8% (n=245), revealing structural abnormalities in 43.6% (n=107). Only 3.7% (n=9) showed acute pathologic findings requiring changes in management. Most abnormalities were chronic and did not influence clinical decisions. The only variable significantly associated with acute CT findings was seizure-related traumatic brain injury (33.3% vs. 0%, P<0.001; OR=26.6, 95% CI: 11.2-62.8).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The diagnostic yield of head CT in patients with nonindex seizures is low despite its widespread use in emergency settings. Routine neuroimaging may be unnecessary without clinical red flags such as trauma, new focal deficits, or atypical presentations. Evidence-based tools are needed to guide neuroimaging use and optimize resource utilization.

articles.title: Management of Self-Harm in Adolescent Inpatient Settings Without Physical Restraint: A Service Evaluation of Physical Health Outcomes from a Least Restrictive Practice Unit.
articles.journal: J Psychosoc Nurs Ment Health Serv
articles.journal_full: Journal of psychosocial nursing and mental health services

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To assess physical health outcomes for young people who self-harmed during admission to a general adolescent unit where physical restraint (PR) is proactively avoided in response to self-harm unless it is immediately life-threatening.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: From the incident reporting system, we extracted data related to self-harm and PR, and calculated the proportion of incidents of self-harm that were managed with PR. We identified what proportion of incidents of self-harm resulted in physical health consequences that required transfer to the emergency department.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were 1,638 incidents of self-harm. PR was used in 20 (1.2%) cases. There were 35 transfers to the emergency department, 15 of which required treatment (0.9% of all self-harm incidents).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These data can inform thresholds for intervention in response to self-harm. There were a large number of self-harm incidents, PR was used in few cases, and the rate of clinically significant acute physical health consequences that required medical treatment was low. These findings support the view that PR in response to self-harm is not necessary in the majority of cases and should be avoided.

articles.title: Factors Associated with Low-Acuity EMS Transport to the Emergency Department: An Observational Study Guided by the Andersen Behavioral Model.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Emergency medical services (EMS) demand is increasing, with a growing proportion of low-acuity encounters. Prior studies are limited by regional sampling, inconsistent definitions, narrow observation periods, and limited theoretical grounding. The objective of this study was to identify predisposing, enabling, and need-based factors associated with EMS transport among low-acuity emergency department (ED) patients, guided by Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a secondary, retrospective observational study using a 10% random sample of multicenter electronic health record data from 21 EDs in the southeastern United States. Eligible visits included: (1) patient age >17 years, (2) occurred between January 1, 2016, and April 29, 2025, (3) triaged as Emergency Severity Index 4 or 5, and (4) ended in a final visit disposition of discharge. The primary outcome was arrival at the ED by EMS. We categorized independent variables as predisposing, enabling, or need-based factors according to Andersen's model. We used multivariable logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 41,761 low-acuity ED encounters, 3,232 (7.7%) arrived by EMS. Higher odds of EMS use were observed for older age (per 10-year increase; aOR 1.33, 95% CI = 1.30-1.36), male sex (aOR 1.20, 95% CI = 1.12-1.30), being retired or disabled (aOR 3.60, 95% CI = 3.15-4.10), being unemployed (aOR 2.26, 95% CI = 2.04-2.52), having a nighttime presentation (aOR 1.63, 95% CI = 1.51-1.76), and mental health diagnosis (aOR 1.76, 95% CI = 1.62-1.90). Lower odds of EMS arrival were observed for white race (aOR 0.89, 95% CI = 0.83-0.96), established primary care (aOR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.53-0.62), weekend presentation (aOR 0.91; 95% CI = 0.84-0.99), and visits during (aOR 0.63, 95% CI = 0.55-0.71) or after (aOR 0.54, 95% CI = 0.48-0.61) the COVID-19 period. Rurality, insurance, and primary language were not associated with EMS use.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among low-acuity ED patients, EMS arrival was associated with older age, unemployment or disability, no established primary care clinician, and a previous mental health diagnosis. These characteristics identify a population that may be served by alternatives to ambulance transport, such as treat-in-place and alternative destination pathways, when paired with expanded access to primary care and behavioral health resources.

articles.title: [Thoracic trauma in Hungary today: heritage, current challenges and future directions].

abstract.text: Thoracic trauma is an important contributor to morbidity and mortality among severely injured patients. While the management of immediately life-threatening intrathoracic injuries is relatively well defined, the treatment of severe blunt chest wall injuries, particularly multiple rib fractures and flail chest, remains variable across institutions. This review aims to summarize the current situation of thoracic trauma care in Hungary, with special emphasis on chest wall injuries and the role of surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF). SSRF should no longer be regarded as an isolated technical procedure, but as part of the complex, multidisciplinary management of patients with rib fractures. Therapeutic decision-making should be based not only on the number of fractured ribs, but also on fracture pattern, chest wall instability, pain, respiratory mechanics, pulmonary parenchymal injury, the patient's physiological reserve, overall injury severity and timing of surgery. The development of thoracic trauma care in Hungary requires a shared indication language, protocol-based imaging, early reassessment, multimodal analgesia, physiotherapy, transparent regional referral pathways and auditable outcome measurement. The existing Hungarian expertise in trauma surgery, thoracic surgery, emergency medicine and intensive care provides a realistic basis for establishing a structured, nationally applicable model of thoracic trauma care. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1686-1692.

articles.title: [Integrated use of ketamine in emergency care].

abstract.text: Ketamine has emerged as a key drug in emergency medicine in recent years due to its rapid onset of action, hemodynamic stability properties and wide applicability. However, Hungarian regulation still limits its use mainly to anesthetic indications. The aim of this study was to review the literature on the emergency use of ketamine, with particular reference to its role in prehospital and intrahospital analgesia, sedation and rapid sequence intubation (RSI) protocols. A structured literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane Library databases, including relevant human studies from 2010 to 2024, and supplemented by selected pre-2010 landmark studies that are pivotal in the historical and clinical context of ketamine use in emergency care. The retrieved publications were thematically categorized, and narrative synthesis was applied. Based on 82 studies reviewed, ketamine was found to be effective and safe in acute analgesia, procedural sedation, agitation management and RSI. Side effects are predominantly mild and well managed. Previous contraindications in patients with head injury are increasingly questioned in the current international literature. The place of ketamine in emergency care is evidence-based. Its use fits well into modern multidisciplinary emergency protocols. It is recommended to update national recommendations in line with international practices. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1679-1685.

articles.title: Outcomes After Major Amputation in Octogenarians.

abstract.text: BackgroundMajor lower extremity amputations, defined as above-ankle amputations, are morbid and significantly life-changing. Older patients may be more susceptible to poor outcomes. Our goal was to assess the short- and long-term outcomes of major amputations in octogenarians.MethodsA retrospective single-center chart review was performed on all octogenarian patients who underwent a major amputation at a safety-net hospital between 2014-2023. Demographics, operative characteristics, postoperative outcomes, and 30-day and 1-year outcomes were collected and analyzed. Multivariable binary logistic regression evaluated factors associated with 1-year mortality. Fisher's exact test evaluated univariate categorical comparisons because of small cell frequencies.Results56 octogenarian patients underwent a major amputation: 96.4% underwent an amputation for chronic limb-threatening ischemia while 3.6% of patients had acute limb ischemia. Above-knee and below-knee amputations accounted for 73.2 and 26.8% of procedures, respectively; 10.6% were guillotine amputations. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was required in 26.3% of cases, and total mean hospital length of stay (LOS) was 13.7 days. Postoperatively, 55.4% were discharged to a skilled nursing facility, 17.9% patients to an acute rehab facility, and 12.5% to home with assistance. Thirty-day emergency department use rate was 14.3%, and hospital readmission rate was 12.5%. Most patients (83.9%) were non-ambulatory at 1-year. In-hospital mortality was 8.9%, 30-day mortality was 14.3%, and 1-year mortality was 35.7%. Univariate analyses demonstrated no statistically significant differences among evaluated variables. Multivariable analysis of 1-year mortality was also not statistically significant.ConclusionMajor amputations in octogenarians are highly morbid with high ICU utilization and prolonged LOS with frequent discharge to acute care facilities. About one-third of patients are not alive at 1-year. These findings suggest the need to identify opportunities for improvement in this high-risk patient population undergoing amputations, such as early revascularization, aggressive rehabilitation in concert with geriatrician collaboration, medical optimization, and improved goals-of-care discussions.

articles.title: [Livedoid vasculopathy: A case report].
articles.journal: Beijing Da Xue Xue Bao Yi Xue Ban
articles.journal_full: Beijing da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Peking University. Health sciences

abstract.text: Livedoid vasculopathy (LV) is a painful and thrombotic obliterative vascular disorder characterized by spontaneous thrombus formation within skin capillaries or small veins, ultimately leading to localized hypoxia and the development of skin ulcers. LV is a rare condition predominantly affecting young women, with an incidence rate of approximately 1/100 000. Clinically, it manifests as recurrent reticular green spots and painful ulcers on the distal lower extremities, which subsequently heal, leaving behind white and atrophic scars, termed "white atrophy". The skin manifestations of the disease are prominent, often seen in dermatology. Recently, the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology of Honghui Hospital, Xi ' an Jiaotong University, admitted a patient with LV. This young female patient presented with recurrent lower limb skin purpura and ulcers, which had occurred spontaneously during the summer for the past three years. Following a skin biopsy conducted at another hospital, she was diagnosed with LV and subsequently treated with phototherapy, anticoagulation therapy, and topical corticosteroids, yet there was no improvement in her condition. In April of this year, she sought further treatment at our hospital and was admitted for comprehensive care. After completing a thorough battery of relevant examinations, we excluded other potential vascular disorders, abnormal coagulation profiles, and autoimmune diseases, such as cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cPAN), leukocyte-cracking vasculitis (LCV), and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). The patient remained definitively diagnosed with LV. Under our department's care, she received oral glucocorticoids, tacrolimus for immune modulation, and colchicine for anti-inflammatory effects. Subsequently, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged from the hospital. Four months post-discharge, a follow-up examination revealed significant improvement in her symptoms. The therapeutic approaches for LV encompassed general therapy, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, glucocorticoid and immunosuppressant therapy, intravenous human immunoglobulin therapy, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Additionally, the use of biologics, including tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and small molecule targeted JAK inhibitors, had been reported in LV cases. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to validate these treatment options. This report presented a case of LV where favorable outcomes were achieved through a combination of anticoagulant and immunosuppressive therapies. Nevertheless, given that the patient has been afflicted with the disease for three years and we have only conducted a four-month follow-up, which is relatively short, continued long-term follow-up of this patient remains imperative.

articles.title: Brain imaging in dystrophinopathies.

abstract.text: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies (DMD, BMD) are caused by genetic variants in the DMD gene coding dystrophin proteins. In addition to the impairment of muscular function, these patients also present frequent cognitive and neuropsychiatric disorders due to impaired expression of several brain dystrophins: Dp427, Dp140 and Dp71. Cerebral imaging has shed new light on the impact of dystrophinopathies on brain structure, function, and connectivity. We review the brain imaging results obtained in patients and divers animal models, showing presence of mild cortical atrophy, slight modifications of structures volumes, decreased cerebral blood flood, white matter microstructure alterations, brain hypometabolism, altered connectivity, and an abnormal cerebral response to stress. We further discuss the putative progression of cerebral disorders, and their variable severity when Dp140 expression is affected in addition to that of Dp427. Some correlations between imaging parameters and cognitive and psychological impairments have been reported but remain to be confirmed.

articles.title: Incidence and predictors of prolonged opioid use following nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma: A national claims-based study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the incidence rates and risk factors of prolonged opioid use following nephrectomy for non-metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC) using a large national insurance database.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Marketscan Commercial Claims and Encounters (MCCD) and Medicare Supplemental (MSD) databases were utilized to identify adult patients who underwent nephrectomy for RCC between 2009 and 2023. Patients with prior malignancy, metastatic disease during or within 12 months after surgery, inadequate insurance coverage, missing data, and opioid use within 90 days before surgery were excluded. The cumulative incidence of prolonged opioid use (≥2 prescriptions or ≥60 days of use between postoperative days 90-365) was determined. Multivariable logistic regression analyzed factors independently associated with prolonged opioid use.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 10,098 patients from the MCCD and 2,980 from MSD were included. About 78% and 65% of patients received opioids during their early postoperative period in the MCCD and MSD databases, respectively. Prolonged opioid use occurred in 8.2% (MCCD) and 9.4% (MSD) of cases. Across both cohorts, higher comorbidity burden, geographic regions, certain insurance types, and greater early postoperative opioid use were independently associated with prolonged opioid use. In the MCCD cohort, female sex, non-metropolitan residence, and early postoperative emergency department visits were additionally associated with prolonged opioid use. Surgical type and operative approach were not significantly associated with the outcome in either cohort.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Almost one in ten patients develops prolonged opioid use following nephrectomy for RCC. Early postoperative opioid exposure appeared strongly associated with prolonged opioid use, demonstrating a clear-dose response relationship. These findings support opioid-sparing strategies and the implementation of perioperative opioid stewardship programs to reduce prolonged opioid use in patients undergoing surgery for non-metastatic RCC.

articles.title: The Impact of Ambient Ozone Exposure on Respiratory Health in the U.S. Populations: A Systematic Review.

abstract.text: Ozone, a photochemically generated air pollutant, continues to pose a major concern for public health in the United States, with some 125 million people living in areas that exceed national ambient air quality standards set by the United States Environmental Protection Agency. To fully understand the potential impacts of ambient ozone exposure on respiratory health, we conducted a systematic review of United States epidemiologic and experimental studies published from 1980 to 2026, encompassing both acute and chronic exposure windows. This review focused on three key domains: (1) pulmonary function, (2) asthma-related symptoms and emergency department visits/hospitalizations, and (3) other respiratory-related morbidity and mortality. Findings across diverse study designs demonstrated adverse respiratory effects, with children, older adults, and individuals with pre-existing respiratory conditions being disproportionately affected. This review is among the first to comprehensively synthesize ozone-related respiratory health outcomes including pulmonary functions outcomes across both experimental and population-based observational studies-highlighting consistent decrements in lung function, even at concentrations below current regulatory standards. Additionally, this work incorporated ozone-associated school absenteeism, a sensitive yet underexamined indicator for pediatric respiratory health outcome. The observed associations across multiple outcomes and exposure durations underscored the importance of strengthening ambient air quality standards and prioritizing interventions toward high-risk populations. Continued increases in ambient ozone exposure even in the presence of regulatory action and increasing contributions from sources related to climate change such as wildfires emphasize the importance of sustained research and public health planning to safeguard respiratory health in vulnerable communities.

articles.title: Intimate Partner Violence and Suicide Risk among Women Presenting to Emergency Departments: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Narrative Synthesis.

abstract.text: Women experiencing intimate partner violence (IPV) and suicide frequently present to emergency departments (EDs). While IPV and suicide are known to co-occur, there is a limited understanding of the intersection in ED presentations. This systematic review, meta-analysis, and narrative synthesis aimed to quantify the association between IPV and suicidality in women presenting to EDs and examine the factors that influence women's suicide risk. Systematic searches of three databases identified 20 ED studies of 7,498 women, reporting associations between IPV and suicidal presentations (final search: 30 August 2025). Pooled prevalence and risk ratios (RRs) were estimated using five random-effects meta-analysis models, stratified by IPV type and suicide-related outcome. Narrative synthesis was used to examine factors associated with suicide risk. Study risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist. On average, 22% (95% CI [0.11, 0.36]) of women with suicide presentations had experienced physical IPV, while 13% [0.08, 0.18] of women with IPV histories reported suicidality. IPV was associated with a three-fold increased risk of suicide attempt (RR 3.00 [1.39, 6.47]), and psychological IPV demonstrated a stronger association (RR 3.23 [1.68, 6.19]) than physical IPV (RR 2.00 [1.26, 3.17]). High between-study heterogeneity was observed across all models (I2 > 75%), and a high risk of bias was identified in half of the studies. The robust associations detected between IPV and suicide attempt underscore the need for contextualised assessment within trauma-informed emergency care to strengthen clinical response and care pathways for women.

articles.title: Impact of Insurance Type on Timing of Diagnosis and Surgical Treatment of Acute Achilles Tendon Ruptures: A 2-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Introduction/PurposeDelayed treatment of acute Achilles tendon rupture is associated with worse outcomes and higher complication rates. Prior studies suggest reduced access to care among Medicaid and uninsured patients. This study examines the effect of insurance status on the timing of diagnosis and surgical treatment among patients undergoing surgical repair of acute Achilles tendon rupture.MethodsA retrospective chart review was conducted of patients aged ≥18 years with acute traumatic Achilles tendon ruptures identified by Current Procedural Terminology codes 27650 and 27654 at 2 hospitals between January 2017 and December 2023. Dates of injury, emergency department presentation, initial outpatient orthopaedic evaluation, and surgical intervention were recorded. Only patients who ultimately underwent operative repair were eligible for inclusion; because case ascertainment relied on surgical procedure codes, the cohort does not capture patients managed nonoperatively or those who never reached surgical care. Insurance status was categorized as private or Medicaid/uninsured. Postoperative complications, including re-rupture, infection, venous thromboembolism, wound dehiscence, return to the operating room, and mortality, were documented. Between-group comparisons of continuous variables were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test, given non-normal distribution of the underlying data; independent 2-tailed t-tests were performed as a secondary, confirmatory analysis. Significance was set at P < .05.ResultsThirty-eight surgically treated patients met the inclusion criteria, including 23 with private insurance and 15 who were Medicaid or uninsured. Median age was 35.2 years, and 89.5% were male. All time intervals are reported as medians. Time from injury to emergency department presentation was longer in the Medicaid/uninsured group but not statistically significant (1.0 vs 0.0 days; Mann-Whitney U P = .079). Medicaid/uninsured patients experienced significantly longer delays from injury to initial outpatient orthopaedic evaluation (17.0 vs 4.0 days; Mann-Whitney U P = .024) and from injury to surgery (30.0 vs 10.0 days; Mann-Whitney U P = .045). Time from orthopaedic evaluation to surgery did not differ significantly between groups (11.0 vs 6.0 days; Mann-Whitney U P = .206). Postoperative complications were infrequent in both groups; the study was not powered for comparison of complication rates and none was performed.ConclusionAmong surgically treated patients, those with Medicaid or no insurance experienced significantly longer delays to initial orthopaedic evaluation and to surgical repair compared with privately insured patients, highlighting disparities in access to timely orthopaedic care within this surgically treated population.Level of Evidence:III.

articles.title: Decompression Sickness Myelopathy: Case Report and Acute Management Review for the Neurologist.

abstract.text: Decompression sickness (DCS) is an uncommon but important cause of acute myelopathy that neurologists should recognize in the emergency setting. We report a 43-year-old experienced technical diver who developed acute sensory loss with a thoracic sensory level, gait dysfunction, upper motor neuron signs, and urinary retention after rapid ascent from approximately 90 feet below sea level. Thoracic spine MRI demonstrated longitudinal, posterior-predominant T2/STIR hyperintensity from T3 to T10-11 without pathologic enhancement, supporting spinal cord DCS. He received prompt hyperbaric oxygen therapy using U.S. Navy Treatment Table 6, along with 100% oxygen, horizontal positioning, and intravenous fluid resuscitation, followed by additional hyperbaric treatments for persistent sensory and autonomic symptoms. He improved rapidly, regained independent ambulation, and later returned to high-level physical activity, although intermittent sensory symptoms persisted during follow-up. This case illustrates the clinical presentation of spinal cord DCS and emphasizes the importance of early hyperbaric oxygen therapy alongside consensus-supported measures for oxygenation, intravascular volume repletion, thermal protection, and safe positioning. The independent effects of these supportive measures on neurologic recovery remain uncertain. Evidence for additional pharmacologic adjuncts, including NSAIDs and corticosteroids, is limited, and cerebrospinal fluid drainage remains unproven in DCS.

articles.title: Mixed Training Team Implementation of the Basic Emergency Care Course in Liberia.

abstract.text: Background: The Basic Emergency Care (BEC) course was developed to improve the management of acute illness and injury in resource-limited settings. Although BEC materials are freely available, formal instructor credentialing requires time and resources that may limit rapid implementation. In remote areas, such as Maryland County, Liberia, innovative approaches to BEC training are needed. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of a BEC course delivered by a mixed instructor team consisting of credentialed and non-credentialed facilitators in improving emergency care knowledge and self-efficacy among healthcare providers in Liberia. Methods: We conducted a mixed-methods evaluation of two consecutive five-day BEC courses held in Maryland County, Liberia, in August 2022. Course participants included physicians, medical interns, physician assistants, and nurses. The instructional team included one credentialed BEC Registered Facilitator and four non-credentialed physician specialists. To promote course fidelity, instructors completed an independent review of course materials, participated in a two-day pre-course preparation workshop, and conducted daily planning and debriefing sessions throughout the training. The effectiveness of this model was evaluated by measuring improvements in participants' emergency care knowledge and confidence using pre- and post-course examinations and self-efficacy surveys. Findings: Participants demonstrated significant improvements in emergency care knowledge, with examination scores increasing from 64.0% pre-course to 86.6% post-course (P < 0.001). Self-efficacy surveys also showed substantial gains in participants' comfort, confidence, and preparedness to manage critically ill and injured patients. Structured instructor preparation and ongoing coordination supported consistent course delivery despite the mixed facilitator model. Conclusions: A BEC course delivered by a mixed team of credentialed and non-credentialed instructors significantly improved emergency care knowledge and self-efficacy among Liberian healthcare providers. This pragmatic, resource-conscious approach may offer a scalable strategy for expanding access to BEC training in remote settings while maintaining course quality and educational effectiveness.

articles.title: Beyond the Earthquake: Cardiovascular Consequences and Lessons for Colombia.

abstract.text: An earthquake is an event that affects populations across multiple dimensions, extending far beyond trauma and immediate mortality. Cardiovascular events are particularly important during the acute phase and in the first days after the disaster, when physiological stress, disruption of healthcare services, medication interruption, and barriers to timely medical attention may increase cardiovascular risk. Previous evidence has documented increases in myocardial infarction, stroke, arrhythmias, cardiovascular mortality, and decompensation of chronic cardiovascular disease following major earthquakes. In Colombia, the recent earthquake affecting Chocó and neighboring regions highlights the particular vulnerability of populations facing geographic isolation and unequal access to healthcare. Disaster preparedness should therefore extend beyond trauma care and include continuity of cardiovascular medications, preservation of emergency referral pathways, capacity to manage sudden increases in cardiovascular demand, and structured follow-up after the acute phase. This article reviews these cardiovascular consequences and discusses their implications for disaster preparedness in Colombia.

articles.title: Association between timely and standardized nursing pain management and outcomes in terminal cancer patients: A retrospective cohort study.

abstract.text: Effective pain management is essential for terminal cancer patients in emergency settings, yet nursing protocol adherence remains suboptimal. This study aimed to evaluate the association between key nursing process indicators and pain relief outcomes in terminal cancer patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) and to examine clinical outcomes according to adherence to an optimized nursing pain management workflow. We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 724 terminal cancer patients who visited the ED of the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University between January 2017 and December 2023. Eligible patients presented with pain as a primary complaint and had complete clinical and nursing documentation. Data were extracted on demographics, cancer type, pain scores, timing of analgesic administration, and reassessment practices. The primary outcome was effective pain relief, defined as a ≥2-point reduction on the numeric rating scale within 1 hour of analgesia. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors. Patients were stratified into an optimized care group (completion of pain assessment within 30 minutes, analgesia within 30 minutes, and reassessment within 1 hour) and a routine care group. Of the 724 patients included, 58.2% achieved effective pain relief. Multivariate analysis revealed that timely pain assessment (odds ratio [OR] = 1.84, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.26-2.69), analgesic administration within 30 minutes (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.57-3.21), opioid use (OR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.06-2.20), and documented pain reassessment (OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.22-2.35) were independently associated with improved pain outcomes. Patients in the optimized care group (n = 286) had significantly higher pain relief rates (75.9% vs 46.6%, P < .001), faster relief onset (29.6 ± 11.3 vs 52.7 ± 15.9 minutes, P < .001), shorter ED stays (3.4 ± 1.1 vs 4.7 ± 1.4 hours, P < .001), and lower 72-hour revisit rates (7.3% vs 21.0%, P < .001). Timely and standardized nursing interventions were associated with more favorable pain relief and emergency department care-efficiency outcomes among terminal cancer patients. These findings support the integration of structured nursing protocols into emergency palliative care, although prospective studies are needed to determine their causal effects.

articles.title: Neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio for predicting delayed neurologic sequelae caused by carbon monoxide poisoning: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: This study summarized and analyzed the prognostic value of the neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR) for delayed neurologic sequelae (DNS) caused by carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure Database were searched to identify relevant articles from their inception to February 2026. The odds ratio and its 95% confidence interval (CI), area under the curve, meta-regression analysis, sensitivity analysis, and publication bias for NLR were estimated to predict DNS.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eight studies were included, involving 1757 patients with acute CO poisoning, among whom 382 cases (21.7%) developed DNS. The pooled results show that NLR was related to DNS (odds ratio = 14.67, 95% CI: 8.26-26.04, P < .001) and had high heterogeneity (I2 = 65.1%, P = .005). The area under the curve of NLR for predicting DNS was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.85-0.91), with a sensitivity of 86% and a specificity of 72%. Subgroup analysis indicated that study design may be the source of heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis suggested the robustness of the results. Deek's test did not detect significant publication bias (P = .24).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Current evidence indicates that an elevated NLR is associated with an increased risk of DNS after acute CO poisoning, supporting its potential utility as a prognostic marker. However, because the included studies showed substantial heterogeneity and were predominantly retrospective, these findings should be interpreted with caution and require validation in high-quality prospective studies. NLR should therefore be considered an auxiliary tool for risk stratification rather than an independent diagnostic method. Its principal clinical value may lie in resource-limited settings where advanced monitoring is not feasible.

articles.title: Validating a Wearable Bluetooth Oximeter for Infants in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit.
articles.journal_full: Journal of paediatrics and child health

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Oxygen is vital for life but the wrong amount of oxygen can lead to significant risk of morbidity and mortality. Preterm infants are at particular risk from both too little (hypoxia) and excess (hyperoxia) oxygen. In the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), oxygen treatment is guided by oximetry derived from wired oximeters which are difficult to use outside of the hospital environment. We aimed to validate Bluetooth wireless oximeters in newborn infants to determine the accuracy of devices that would be more suitable for out of hospital use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Three 20 min sets of measurements including oxygen saturations (SpO2), heart rate (HR) and perfusion index (PI) from the post-ductal regions (left arm and lower limbs) were conducted in 21 spontaneously ventilating infants using the Masimo (1) SafetyNet and (2) Radical 7 oximeters. The wired Radical 7 oximeter was the reference. Data were downloaded onto CSV files and analysed for agreement.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-one (eight male) infants were recruited between July to September 2023. Median gestations and ages were 36 weeks and 3 days. Neither Bluetooth device (SafetyNet and wireless Radical 7) met International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard (ARMSE ≤ 3%), Score 3.624 (wireless Rad-7) and 3.884 (SafetyNet). Both wearables consistently overestimated SpO2, with mean biases (wired-wearable) of -1.802 (Rad-7) and -1.803 (SafetyNet), that increased at lower SpO2 levels. Linear regression, ICC, Pearson's correlation analyses showed poor consistency.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Wireless oximeters have poor correlation with wired oximeters especially at lower SpO2 levels but ease of use, especially in the home environment in less acutely ill patients, requires further evaluation.

articles.title: Improving Spanish-Speaking Caregivers' Experience with Standardized Discharge Instructions for Asthma Exacerbation in the Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pediatric asthma is a leading cause of emergency department (ED) utilization, with higher rates among minority populations. Families with limited English proficiency, particularly Spanish-speaking caregivers, may face discharge communication barriers that contribute to outcome disparities.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe Spanish-speaking caregiver-reported experiences with discharge communication and follow-up support after receipt of a standardized Spanish-language asthma discharge protocol and to explore 72-hour ED revisit rates among participating patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective observational study of Spanish-speaking caregivers of children presenting with asthma exacerbations to a tertiary pediatric ED between April 2023 and March 2025. Caregivers completed a REDCap survey assessing demographics, language preferences, interpreter use, discharge communication, and follow-up support. The primary outcome was return ED visits for asthma exacerbation within 72 h, compared with a pediatric ED population using Fisher's exact test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fifty-four Spanish-speaking caregivers were included. Most preferred discharge instructions in Spanish (94.4%); 30% reported effective English communication. Although satisfaction with interpreter services (92.0%) and provider explanations of asthma (92.6%) was high, 61.1% needed help scheduling follow-up appointments. Contributors to discharge confusion included provider time (23.1%), terminology (15.4%), and language barriers (15.4%). The surveyed group had a significantly higher 72-hour ED revisit rate than the control population (7.7% vs. 2.1%, p = 0.039).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Despite high satisfaction with interpreter services and provider explanations, gaps remained in follow-up support. The participating group also had a higher 72-hour revisit rate; however, the observational design cannot determine whether discharge communication or the standardized protocol contributed to this difference.

articles.title: An Accountable Encounter-Based Imaging Workflow for Point-of-Care Ultrasound: Integrating Image Availability, Clinician Attribution, and Documentation Accountability.
articles.journal_full: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine

abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is integral to emergency department (ED) care, but traditional order-based imaging workflows (OBIWs) are poorly aligned with unscheduled encounters and dynamic bedside imaging needs. We describe an accountable encounter-based imaging workflow (EBIW) that integrates patient identification, clinician attribution, encounter-linked image routing, and documentation accountability into a unified imaging informatics architecture. We performed a retrospective observational analysis of aggregated ED POCUS charge data from January 2018 through December 2025 at a single urban academic ED. Three sequential workflows were evaluated: a legacy electronic health record (EHR)-based OBIW, a POCUS Manager-based OBIW, and an accountable EBIW. The accountable EBIW links ultrasound images directly to the ED encounter using barcode-based patient and clinician identification and a centralized Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) router that generates an image availability message. This enables immediate image access in the picture archiving and communication system, EHR, and POCUS management platform before report completion. Charges were not used as a measure of reimbursement or financial return. Because a charge could only be generated after image archival, encounter linkage, documentation, and clinician attestation, charge capture served as a longitudinal system-level marker of completed workflow execution. Charges were normalized by ED visit volume and analyzed using interrupted time series analysis. Transition from the EHR-based OBIW to the POCUS Manager-based OBIW was not associated with an immediate increase in charges. Implementation of the accountable EBIW was associated with an immediate level increase of $11,746 per 1000 visits and a sustained positive quarterly slope thereafter. An accountable EBIW integrating encounter-level acquisition, DICOM routing, immediate image availability, clinician attribution, and documentation accountability was associated with improved capture of ED POCUS utilization.

articles.title: The role of low muscle strength in predicting mortality in patients with liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

abstract.text: Sarcopenia is a prevalent complication in chronic liver disease (CLD), traditionally assessed by muscle mass. Recent paradigm shifts focus to dynapenia as the primary determinant of adverse outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the role of dynapenia, as measured by handgrip strength (HGS) and ultrasound-derived diaphragmatic excursion, in predicting mortality in this population. This prospective study included consecutive outpatients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma history attending a tertiary hepatology unit. Muscle mass was assessed in subgroups using bioimpedance analysis (BIA) and computed tomography (CT). Associations between sarcopenia proxies and 24-month all-cause mortality were analyzed with adjusted Cox regression models, and survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves. Ninety-one patients were included (age 73.4 ± 8.1 years; 71 [78%] male); 20 (22%) had dynapenia. Twenty-two deaths occurred at two years (24.2%). Over 24 months, dynapenia (by HGS) and diaphragmatic excursion were associated with mortality in adjusted models (aHR 1.68, 95% CI 1.12-2.53, p = 0.012; aHR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.97, p = 0.042). In subgroups, they remained the only muscle parameters associated with mortality, while muscle mass indices were not significant. Finally, Kaplan-Meier estimates showed lower 24-month survival in dynapenic patients across groups (in overall population 65% vs. 79%, p = 0.05). Low muscle strength is a key prognostic parameter in patients with cirrhosis and HCC. In our small cohort, it was the only muscle-related measure significantly associated with mortality. These findings support further evaluation of muscle strength assessment as a potential tool for risk stratification in this population.

articles.title: Physiotherapy contact in the emergency department and hospital re‑presentation rates: A systematic review and meta‑regression.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To determine if physiotherapy input in the Emergency Department (ED) impacts patient re-presentation rates.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Three electronic databases (Medline (Ovid), EMBASE (Ovid) and CINAHL) were searched from inception to November 16th, 2025. Included articles were peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials, observational studies or audits evaluating re-presentation rates for physiotherapy intervention in ED compared to an ED physician. Risk of bias was assessed using The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) tool was used to assess level of evidence for the meta-analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Sixteen studies were included in the systematic review. Overall pooled results from ten studies included in the 30-day re-presentation meta-analysis provided low-quality evidence of no difference in the risk of re-presentation following physiotherapy intervention compared with ED physician management (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.69-1.55).
