Subgroup analysis by presenting condition demonstrated a lower risk of 30-day re-presentation following physiotherapy intervention for fall presentations (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.59-0.74), with no differences observed for musculoskeletal presentations (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.61-2.22) or general ED presentations (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.66-1.33) compared with ED physician management.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Irrespective of included condition, physiotherapy intervention in ED does not increase the risk of re-presentation within 30 days of initial presentation, and potentially reduces re-presentation rates for fall patients. Further research is required to determine the most effective component of physiotherapy intervention to reduce re-presentation rates and its impact on ED crowding.

articles.title: Project international Delphi consensus recommendations for perioperative management of inguinal lymphadenectomy in cancer patients.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To establish international expert consensus on perioperative strategies for the prevention, management, and follow-up of complications related to inguinal lymph node dissection.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This international modified Delphi consensus study was conducted between September 2025 and March 2026 using a 2-round electronic survey. A total of 101 experts from 25 countries participated, including urologists, surgical oncologists, plastic surgeons, and other specialists with experience in ILND for penile cancer, melanoma, and vulvar cancer. Eighty-six clinical statements addressing ILND-associated complications were evaluated across 6 domains: preoperative nutritional optimization, anemia management, lymphatic complications, infectious and cutaneous complications, vascular and musculoskeletal complications, and functional rehabilitation. Agreement was assessed using a 5-point Likert scale, with consensus defined a priori as at least 70% of participants selecting "somewhat agree" or "strongly agree."

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Consensus was achieved for 51 of 86 statements. Agreed recommendations supported standardized approaches to preoperative nutritional assessment and anemia correction, prevention and management of lymphatic complications, drain placement and management, discharge criteria, antibiotic prophylaxis, wound complication management, thromboprophylaxis, multimodal analgesia, and early functional rehabilitation. No consensus was reached regarding routine use of immunonutrition, optimal duration of antibiotic therapy, topical treatments, muscle relaxants, or hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This international Delphi process generated consensus-based, multidisciplinary recommendations to guide perioperative ILND management. These statements may provide a structured framework to support greater standardization of perioperative care pathways across malignancies requiring ILND, reduce morbidity, and inform quality-improvement initiatives. Prospective validation is required to evaluate their clinical impact and refine areas of ongoing uncertainty.

articles.title: Does performing preprocedural point-of-care ultrasound improve success rate for lumbar punctures in paediatric patients?
Flu and covid: Respiratory illnesses pile pressure on ambulances and hospitals.
The Underwater Mindset in Emergency Surgery.

abstract.text: Emergency surgery requires decision-making in environments characterized by uncertainty, evolving conditions, and narrowing margins of safety. Scuba diving presents similar challenges, requiring continuous reassessment of the environment, individual capacity, equipment, and team while preserving sufficient reserve to respond to unexpected events. This Surgical Reflection uses the underwater environment as a conceptual framework to explore adaptive expertise in emergency surgery. Three interconnected capabilities are considered: maintaining situational awareness beyond the immediate technical task, preserving cognitive reserve and team function as workload increases, and recognizing when persistence should give way to a change in strategy. The underwater mindset reframes adaptation-including conversion, damage-control approaches, seeking additional expertise, or abandoning an unsafe operative plan-not as failure, but as an expression of surgical judgment. In dynamic high-risk environments, expertise may ultimately depend not only on the ability to proceed, but on recognizing when the conditions that justified the original plan have changed.

articles.title: When is travel-health AI inference transportable? Mobility-conditioned admissibility for cross-border disease risk and decision support.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for infectious disease surveillance, traveller risk assessment, outbreak forecasting and decision support. Travel creates a distinctive transportability problem because people move between epidemiological, geographic, climatic and healthcare contexts in which the conditions supporting an inference may change rapidly.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This conceptual/theoretical methodological-development study was informed by a targeted narrative review of travel medicine, infectious disease surveillance, human mobility, border health, mass gatherings, antimicrobial resistance and health-AI validation literature.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We develop a mobility-conditioned admissibility framework that treats travel as movement across origin, transit, destination and return regimes. Interpretation is conditioned on mobility state, epidemiological regime, exposure history, time-dependent constraints and clinical or biological constraints. Five proposed operational states are retained: supported inference, conditionally transportable inference, active monitoring, restricted interpretation and withholding. The framework also distinguishes low probability from infeasibility and requires preservation of rare but epidemiologically feasible events.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Model availability and conventional predictive validity do not establish inferential transportability across changing travel contexts. Mobility-conditioned admissibility provides a complementary use-boundary layer for travel health AI by making cross-regime support explicit before outputs are interpreted or released. Its incremental value requires prospective evaluation against calibrated uncertainty, external validation and dataset-shift monitoring.

articles.title: Implementing a Portable, Simulation-Based Trauma Curriculum for Rural Hospitals: Planning Pilot Year.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Trauma patients receiving care in rural settings face higher mortality rates than those at tertiary referral centers. Rural hospitals experience significant gaps in trauma care from limited access to specialists, procedural training, and standardized team-based education. In Georgia, over 20% of trauma patients come from rural areas where high-fidelity trauma training is limited. To address these disparities, we developed a trauma simulation curriculum for rural Georgia trauma providers.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A mixed-methods needs assessment was conducted to identify training needs reported by rural trauma providers. A modular simulation curriculum was created to address common deficiencies in procedural skills, interdisciplinary communication, and trauma system activations. The pilot curriculum was presented at a rural trauma conference by a multidisciplinary team, including interactive lectures and hands-on procedural skills stations (airway management, hemorrhage control, and chest trauma).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The needs assessment revealed training gaps in airway management, tube thoracostomy, cervical collar placement, hemorrhage control, and transfusion guidelines. The curriculum consisted of didactics and simulation sessions grounded in educational strategies (Cognitive Learning Theory, Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and Simulation-Based Learning). Participants included rural providers from emergency medical services, nursing, respiratory therapy, and physicians. Learners reported high satisfaction with interactive didactics, hands-on simulation, and interdisciplinary learning.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: We developed a multidisciplinary rural trauma simulation curriculum. Early implementation and participant feedback guided iterative refinement, optimizing didactic content, assessment methods, and simulation tasks. This initiative addresses a significant gap in rural trauma readiness and offers a scalable, sustainable model for multidisciplinary trauma education in resource-limited environments.

articles.title: Trends in mortality rates in hypotensive pediatric trauma patients undergoing emergent trauma laparotomy.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Massive hemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable death after pediatric trauma. Emergent trauma laparotomy (ETL) is a common operation to obtain hemorrhage control. Mortality rates for adult patients in hemorrhagic shock requiring ETL remain high and unchanged. Information on mortality rates after ETL in pediatric patients is limited. We sought to evaluate trends in mortality rates for pediatric ETL patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The National Trauma Data Bank (NTDB) was queried from 2007 to 2023. Patients aged 0 to 18 years old were included if they underwent ETL. ETL was defined as laparotomy within 1 hour of arrival. Hypotension was defined as a systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg on arrival. The primary outcome was annual hospital mortality rates for hypotensive patients requiring ETL. Secondary outcomes included annual 24-hour mortality rates for both hypotensive and all patients requiring ETL. Mortality rates were compared in 5-year cohorts to reduce annual variability.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 11,374 patients underwent ETL. The majority of patients were male (79%; n=78,963/11,374). Most patients were between the ages of 12 and 17 (84%; n=9,565/11,374), followed by ages 5 to 11 (11%; n=1,227/11,374), then ages 0 to 4 (5%; n=582/11,374). Penetrating injuries predominated (69%; n=7,866/11,374). The hospital mortality rate for all patients was 18.3% (n=2,079/11,374). Of patients who died, 74% were within 24 hours of arrival (n=1,533/2,079). Overall, 19% (n=2,125/11,374) were hypotensive on arrival. For hypotensive patients, the 24-hour and hospital mortality rates were 30% (n=641/2,125) and 45.9% (n=976/2,125). There was year-to-year variability in rates of hospital mortality of hypotensive patients through the study period (p<0.001). However, the average mortality rates from 2007 to 2011 (45%; n=293/645) and 2019 to 2023 (42%; n=266/638) were unchanged (p=0.95).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Pediatric trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage requiring ETL continue to suffer high rates of mortality. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted research and performance improvement.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: Opioid prescribing and hospital outcomes after trauma in patients with substance use disorder: An analysis of the michigan trauma quality improvement project.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Trauma patients frequently have comorbid substance use disorders (SUD), which may complicate pain management and increase the risk of opioid-related adverse outcomes after discharge. We hypothesized that trauma patients with SUD would be prescribed more opioids at discharge than those without SUD.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We retrospectively analyzed a cohort of adult trauma patients across the state from 2022 to 2025 using a statewide collaborative database. Primary outcomes were opioid prescription at discharge (yes/no) and amount prescribed standardized to oxycodone 5 mg pills. A multivariable approach assessed risk-adjusted differences in outcomes among patients with SUD versus without SUD.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 29,805 total patients, 8,672 (29.1%) had a diagnosis of SUD. 71.2% of patients with SUD received a discharge opioid prescription, compared with 59.6% of patients without SUD (p<0.001). After adjustment, the predicted probability of receiving an opioid prescription at discharge was 64.2% (95% CI, 63.1%-65.2%) for patients with SUD and 62.5% (95% CI, 62.0%-63.1%) for those without. Among patients that received a prescription, those with SUD were prescribed 21.2 pills of 5 mg oxycodone, corresponding to an adjusted difference of 1.6 additional pills (95% CI, 0.89-2.31; p<0.001) compared with those without. Prescribing patterns also differed by race and ethnicity: Hispanic or Latino patients were 5.4-percentage points more likely to receive an opioid prescription than non-Hispanic or Latino patients, while, among prescription recipients, Black patients received 3.56 fewer pills than White patients.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Our findings demonstrate that patients with SUD received opioids more frequently and in greater amounts at discharge, yet absolute differences were small in magnitude and may not represent clinically meaningful differences. Differences in prescribing by race and ethnicity were larger in magnitude and warrant further investigation.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Prognostic and epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: In older adults, "mild" by GCS does not mean low risk: Multicenter study of 1,157 patients with mild TBI and acute subdural hematoma.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
authors: Traumatic Subdural Hematoma Outcomes Study Group

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) is the most common intracranial injury in mild TBI (mTBI), particularly in older adults. However, the relationship of patient and brain computed tomography (CT) characteristics with outcomes remains poorly described in a contemporary cohort. This study aims to characterize outcomes in younger and older adults with mTBI and isolated acute SDH.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a 10-center, retrospective cohort study of adult traumas with emergency department Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 13 to 15 and acute traumatic SDH on initial brain CT ('22-'23). Trauma registry, EHR, and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) data were collected through automated and manual methods. The primary outcome was total mortality (TM=death+hospice discharge); the sample was stratified by 18 to 64 versus older than or equal to 65 years. Multivariable backward selection logistic regression examined 21 demographic, injury, and brain CT covariates.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In total, 1,157 patients were included (18-64 y: 28%; ≥65 y: 72%; 58% transferred in). Median [IQR] non-head ISS was 1 [1-5] in 18 to 64 years, and 1 [1-2] in older than or equal to 65 years. Ten percent had neurosurgical intervention (18-64 y: 8%; ≥65 y: 11%). TM was higher in older than or equal to 65 years than 18 to 64 years (10% vs. 3%). Compared with older than or equal to 65 years, 18 to 64 years were discharged home more frequently (78% vs. 51%) and to hospice less frequently (2% vs. 7%). In 18 to 64 years, factors associated with TM were race, advance directive, functional dependence, ISS, more midline shift, and thicker SDH (too few TMs for adjusted models). In older than or equal to 65 years, factors independently associated with TM were advance directive (aOR [95% CI]: 11.8 [2.9-49.0]), male sex (3.0 [1.3-7.0]), midline shift (1.8 [1.3-2.6]), shock index (1.5 [1.1-2.1]), and worsening SDH on follow-up CT (2.9 [1.3-6.6]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Despite presenting as "mild", these data highlight that older adults with SDH have high TM and should continue to receive the highest-level care with timely goals-of-care discussions. The association between advance directives and TM should be interpreted within the context of baseline vulnerability and preinjury treatment preferences, not as a biological mortality predictor.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: Early hospital discharge following delivery during wartime is not associated with increased rates of postpartum hospital referrals.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: During war, significant adaptations take place in hospitals to improve the treatment of soldiers and civilians. For example, low-risk women were discharged earlier from hospitals following delivery. The aim of the study was to compare the rate of postpartum-visits to the gynecological-emergency-room (GER) between wartime to a similar period in the previous year.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective study compared the visits of postpartum-women in the GER to a similar period in the previous year.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The study included 801 women who delivered in the first month of the war in 2023 and 913 who delivered in the parallel period in the previous year. There were no significant changes in maternal age, gravidity, parity, mode of delivery, birthweight, meconium, low Apgar scores, and the rate of admissions to the neonatal intensive care unit. There were significantly less elective cesarean sections during wartime (57% vs. 92%; p < 0.0001). The duration of postpartum hospitalization was significantly shorter during wartime [median length of 53.2 [Interquartile-range (IQR] 42.4-72.4) hours vs. 64.1 (IQR 47.4-82.8) in the previous year (p < 0.0001)]. There were no significant differences in the rate of total referrals of postpartum-women to the GER (8.7% vs. 8.8%; p > 0.05), and no differences in referrals due to infections or bleeding. There was no difference in the rate of admission of postpartum-women (17% vs. 14%; p = 0.73).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Shortening of hospitalization following delivery during war is feasible, does not cause increase postpartum visits to the GER, and does not increase GER visits due to infections or bleeding.

articles.title: Unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries: Insights from 3473 births of a 13-year prospective cohort study in France.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Although poorly researched, unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries are considered to carry a high risk of maternal and neonatal complications, with the primary suspected risk factor being the home-to-hospital travel time. The objective of this study was to describe the characteristics of unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries and to identify factors associated with maternal and neonatal complications.

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected from the French unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries registry (79 of 402 mobile intensive care units). Analysis included 3473 deliveries between October 2011 and June 2024.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean women maternal age was 32.0 ± 5.4 years (range 15-49). Median parity was 2.0 (IQR 2.0-3.0). Gestational age was 39.1 ± 2.3 weeks. Most pregnancies were low-risk (84%). Mean home-to-hospital travel time was 20.7 ± 13.6 min (range 0-200), with more than 45 min for only 3% of women (110/3221) and over 1 h for 1% (23/3221). Maternal complications accounted in 8.4% of women (290/3472), placental hemorrhage in 4.5% (156/3471) and maternal death in 0.1% (2/3471). Perinatal complications occurred in 4.4% (149/3393) of all deliveries, with neonatal deaths accounting for 1.1% (38/3456). Among unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries, factors associated with maternal and/or neonatal complications included birth at 32 + 0-33 + 6 weeks of gestation (adjusted OR 2.86, 95% CI 1.69 to 4.83; p < 0.0001), birth before 32 + 0 weeks of gestation (adjusted OR 25.21, 95% CI 12.13 to 52.40; p < 0.0001), and neonatal hypothermia upon hospital admission (adjusted OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.76; p = 0.019). Hypothermia affected 63% of newborns (1256/2002). Unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries prior to mobile intensive care unit arrival were significantly associated with neonatal hypothermia on-site (adjusted OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.57 to 2.61; p < 0.0001) and at hospital admission (adjusted OR 1.56, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.00; p = 0.0005).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Severe outcomes of unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries were uncommon but did occur. Complications were associated with prematurity and hypothermia, but not with home-to-hospital travel time. These findings highlight the importance of universal prehospital preparedness, with particular attention to early prevention of neonatal hypothermia and initial hemorrhage management.

articles.title: Decreasing response phase lights and siren use through modification of dispatch priority response for 9-1-1 responses to personal emergency response system activations: an interventional study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Emergency medical services (EMS) responses to personal emergency response systems (PERS) activations predominantly involve low-acuity patients. Recent evidence demonstrates that while most PERS calls are dispatched lights and siren (L&S), only 1% result in L&S transport. Reduction of L&S use through modified dispatch priority response for PERS calls has not been evaluated. Our objective was to evaluate the efficacy of modifying dispatch priority response mode for PERS calls to non-L&S response, the resulting reduction in response phase L&S use, and potential impact on time critical interventions.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective observational pre-post analysis comparing PERS responses in two 11-month periods before (January-November 2023) and after (January-November 2024) revising the dispatch priority response for PERS calls to non-L&S in December 2023. We evaluated response mode and transport mode. The primary outcome was total hours/month of response phase L&S use, with L&S duration computed as the interval between unit dispatched and arrival (patient contact) or call cancellation. Descriptive statistics were computed followed by interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) to assess the impact of the intervention on the primary outcome and maintenance of the effect across the post-intervention period (p for post-intervention linear trend).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Analysis included 3,262 PERS calls (pre-intervention = 1,634; post-intervention = 1,628). L&S response occurred in 98% (n = 1,601) of pre-intervention calls and 12% (n = 192) of post-intervention calls (p < 0.001). The prevalence of L&S transport was similar in both periods (0.9% vs 0.9%, p = 0.99). The ITSA revealed an immediate 13.8-hour/month decrease in response phase L&S use (95% confidence interval: -16.2 to -11.3) that was sustained across the post-intervention period (p > 0.05). Total response phase L&S hours decreased 86%, from 172 hours in the pre-intervention period to 24 hours during the post-intervention period. Importantly, only four post-intervention calls (0.2%) involved a non-L&S response followed by L&S transport, with just one of these requiring advanced life support interventions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Modifying dispatch priority response for PERS calls reduced L&S responses and yielded a marked decrease in hours of L&S use which was maintained overtime. As the industry advocates for safer, more judicious L&S use, additional low-acuity call types should be identified for similar dispatch priority response revision.

articles.title: In-Simulation Versus Post-Simulation Debriefing in Medical Training: A Scoping Review and Theoretical Framework for Military Application.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Simulation-based medical training is important for readiness. Feedback and debriefing are important components of simulation that support learning. Debriefs for military training are traditionally conducted at the conclusion of training, but recent evidence in the civilian medical training literature suggests that in-simulation debriefing may provide benefits for skill acquisition. The purpose of this scoping review is to map the body of literature examining post-simulation and in-simulation debriefing, highlight trends in the literature, and identify research gaps.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A scoping review of the literature was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute Scoping Review Methodology, searching PubMed, the Web of Science Core Collection, and gray literature. Studies were included if they evaluated simulation-based emergency medicine or critical care medical training with an in-simulation debriefing intervention compared to post-simulation debriefing, measured at least one learning or performance outcome, and included a randomization element. Studies were excluded if they lacked a comparison group, involved non-acute care, utilized solely device-generated feedback, or did not explicitly articulate in-simulation debriefing protocols.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 21 articles met inclusion criteria; none involved military populations. The majority of studies (90.5%) employed rapid cycle deliberate practice as the in-simulation debriefing method, and the most studied domain was cardiac arrest and resuscitation (57.1%). No studies reported performance or retention measures favoring post-simulation debriefing, and 77.8% of studies measuring time to intervention found significant improvements when in-simulation debriefing was utilized. Effect sizes were only reported in 14.3% of included studies.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The majority of reviewed studies reported outcomes favoring in-simulation debriefing; no studies favored post-simulation debriefing for performance measures. Effective implementation of in-simulation debriefing in a military training context would require deliberate instructor development and standardized methods for aligning debriefing methods with the experience level of the target audience. Future research should examine the effects of in-simulation debriefing on tactical medical skill performance and the time to intervention in a military training context.

articles.title: Riders of hired vs privately-owned e-scooters: comparison of injury presentations to emergency departments and implications for prevention.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Prospective patient survey comparing profiles of riders injured using hired versus privately owned e-scooters across four major Queensland hospitals.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Multicenter prospective cohort study of emergency department presentations (May 2024-June 2025) involving e-scooter riders aged ≥16 years. Univariate generalized linear regression used to screen predictors of ownership type (hire vs private), followed by multivariable binary logistic regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 218 eligible cases, 190 (87.2%) had complete data and were included in multivariable analyses. Infrequent e-scooter use was strongly associated with hire use. Compared with frequent users (6+ days/week), participants who rode once per week had substantially higher odds of being injured while using a hire e-scooter rather than a private e-scooter (OR 19.8, 95% CI 4.6-84.8). Riding at >25 km/h was associated with lower odds of hire use compared with ≤12 km/h (OR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.23). Bruising/abrasions (vs fracture) were strongly associated with hire use (OR 15.2, 95% CI 3.6-64.1). Hire use was also more likely among participants who would have otherwise walked if an e-scooter were unavailable (OR 4.9, 95% CI 1.9-12.9) and those who had consumed alcohol prior to the incident (OR 10.0, 95% CI 2.0-51.0). Finally, late night injuries were more prevalent in hire scooters.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: While database/chart audit studies provide insights into the patterns of e-scooter injuries, it is only through data collection directly with patients can a more nuanced understanding of ownership profiles be established. Findings support targeted prevention, infrastructure and policy measures tailored to ownership profiles.

articles.title: Systemic nicotine exposure following switching to heated tobacco products: a category-level analysis of urinary nicotine equivalents.
Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Early Pregnancy Loss (EPL) Among U.S. Emergency Department Visits: The Compounding Role of Advanced Maternal Age.
articles.journal_full: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Early pregnancy loss (EPL) is one of the most prevalent pregnancy complications in the United States, with maternal age consistently identified as a key correlate. However, limited evidence exists regarding the influence of racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disadvantage on the settings in which EPL is managed.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective observational study utilized the 2019 Nationwide Emergency Department Sample. The analytic sample included pregnancy-related emergency department visits by individuals aged 15 to 49 years. The primary outcome was the presence of an ICD-10-CM diagnosis code for EPL (O03.x) during a visit, rather than the actual occurrence of EPL. Key exposures included maternal age and race and ethnicity. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were adjusted for insurance type, patient location, and hospital and visit characteristics.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 889,060 pregnancy-related ED visits, 43,275 (4.9%) carried an EPL diagnosis code (mean age, 28.8 vs. 27.2 years; p < 0.001). Visits by individuals aged 35 years and older demonstrated higher odds of EPL coding than those aged 15-24 years (aOR 2.26; 95% CI 2.17-2.34). Elevated odds were likewise observed among Hispanic (aOR 1.27; 1.19-1.35) and Asian/Pacific Islander (aOR 1.15; 1.03-1.28) pregnant individuals relative to White pregnant individuals, and among self-pay visits (aOR 2.28; 2.05-2.53). Regional and rural-urban differences were pronounced, and no age-by-race and ethnicity interaction was statistically significant.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Racial, ethnic, insurance-related, and geographic differences in EPL-coded ED visits were evident in 2019 and operated across the age distribution rather than widening at AMA. These estimates establish a pre-Dobbs, pre-pandemic baseline against which subsequent shifts in EPL-related emergency care may be evaluated.

articles.title: Missed Nursing Care in the Emergency Department: A Qualitative Interview Study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency departments are high-risk settings for missed nursing care, which jeopardizes patient safety and nurses' physical and mental well-being. However, specific manifestations, multifaceted factors, and consequences of missed nursing care in emergency departments require further investigation. This study aims to explore the manifestations, multifaceted factors, and consequences of missed nursing care in the emergency department to guide quality improvement.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Semistructured interviews were conducted from December 2025 to February 2026, with participants recruited via purposive sampling. The sample comprised 5 emergency nursing leaders, 14 emergency clinical nurses, and 5 emergency patients. Interview data were sorted and coded in NVivo 12 and analyzed following Colaizzi's 7-step phenomenological approach to extract core themes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The analysis identified 9 themes and 34 subthemes, systematically revealing the manifestations, causes, and impacts of missed nursing care in the emergency department. Missed nursing care content included: time-sensitive interruptions to critical care and life support; challenges and omissions in fundamental and therapeutic nursing care; and rigidity of assessment, observation, and documentation. Contributing factors were categorized into system and resource factors, team and individual nursing factors, and patient and clinical characteristics. Participants reported consequences affecting patients, nurses, and hospitals.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Missed nursing care in the emergency department represents a multifaceted phenomenon driven by multifactorial causes specific to the emergency context. Given its severe clinical consequences, clinical leaders must implement targeted interventions to address the root causes of missed nursing care, thereby safeguarding patient safety and improving nursing practice.

articles.title: Multidomain Post-Concussive Symptom Trajectories and Biopsychosocial Correlates Following Pediatric Concussion.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Understanding how post-concussive symptoms (PCS) evolve across multiple domains and how these patterns relate to biopsychosocial factors is critical for identifying children at risk of prolonged recovery following concussion.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To identify clinically meaningful recovery groups characterized by shared trajectories of cognitive, physical, emotional, and fatigue PCS over 3 months post-injury, and to examine associations between trajectory group membership and pre-injury, injury-related, and biopsychosocial factors.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted at the Royal Children's Hospital, Victoria, Australia. Participants were children aged 5-18 years presenting to the emergency department (ED) with concussion.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: Cognitive, physical, emotional, and fatigue PCS above pre-injury baseline were assessed via parent report using the Postconcussion Symptom Inventory at ED presentation and at 2-4 days, 2 weeks, 1 month, and 3 months post-injury. Group-based multi-trajectory modeling identified recovery groups. Associations with pre-injury, injury-related, psychosocial, and child factors were examined.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 326 children (231 males [70.9%]; mean [SD] age, 11.6 [3.2] years), five recovery trajectories were identified: resilient (n = 45, 14%), early recovery (n = 28, 9%), typical recovery (n = 146, 45%), delayed symptom exacerbation (n = 24, 7%), and persistently high symptom endorsement (n = 83, 25%). Exploratory comparisons suggested that persisting trajectories were associated with prior child mental health history and greater post-injury psychosocial difficulties.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: Pediatric concussion symptom domains followed broadly similar time courses for most children; however, among children with delayed or persisting symptoms, some domains differed in the shape and timing of change. Recovery profiles characterized by persisting symptom endorsement were more strongly associated with psychosocial and mental health factors than with injury-related characteristics, underscoring the importance of early psychosocial screening and ongoing monitoring.

articles.title: From Uniformity to Need-Adaptive Capacity: A Scalable Model for Equitable Mental Health and Psychosocial Support After Disasters.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: This Letter addresses a critical operational gap in disaster mental health and psychosocial support: how to deploy limited specialist capacity dynamically without fragmenting services. Evidence confirms substantial disparities in disaster-related mental health outcomes and identifies MHPSS, assessment, referral, and community engagement as core humanitarian response components. Yet a clear mechanism for allocating these components based on changing needs remains underdeveloped. We propose a need-adaptive model that standardizes the service backbone while adjusting specialist intensity according to operational signals. The model operates through four actions: assess for action--brief, decision-oriented assessment, as demonstrated by CASPER following the Eastern Kentucky floods; match tasks to complexity--frontline non-specialists provide basic care while specialists focus on complex cases, supported by meta-analytic evidence showing significant improvements in PTSD symptoms, deploy by threshold, not geography--a mobile multidisciplinary unit responding to predefined signals, and adapt delivery while preserving standards--local partners shaping culturally appropriate care. This approach reframes the equity question from "Which intervention should each subgroup receive?" to "What level of expertise is needed, where, and for how long?" The model reconciles equity with operational feasibility, is testable through implementation research, and offers a practical pathway from contextualized MHPSS principles to scalable field deployment.

articles.title: Developing the Universal Child Abuse Screening Tool (U-CAST) for Epic: A Qualitative Analysis of Expert Working Groups.

abstract.text: Child abuse and maltreatment remain major public health concerns in the United States. Early identification is challenging, particularly for clinicians without specialized pediatric training, and disparities in detection raise concerns about bias. Universal screening integrated into electronic health records (EHRs) may improve detection and equity. To develop an evidence-based, user-friendly, and broadly applicable universal child abuse screening tool (U-CAST) for integration into the EPIC Foundation System. A qualitative study engaged nine expert working groups comprising 17 specialists in child abuse pediatrics, pediatric trauma surgery, general pediatrics, and pediatric emergency medicine. Between February and April 2022, groups met virtually to discuss screening content, clinical decision support, workflow integration, and implementation considerations. Meeting transcripts were analyzed using inductive coding and thematic analysis. Five themes emerged: (1) the importance of universal screening; (2) essential tool components; (3) appropriate clinical settings; (4) actionable follow-up protocols for positive screens; and (5) local program evaluation. Preliminary implementation data demonstrated successful integration, high screening completion rates, and encouraging performance in identifying children with suspected physical abuse. U-CAST was developed through a multi-disciplinary expert process and designed for integration into Epic workflows. Preliminary findings support its feasibility and clinical utility.

articles.title: From Strategic Oversight to Frontline Care: Nursing Leadership in Hospital at Home Deployment During Conflict.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: During Israel's recent "Lion's Roar" conflict, health care systems faced an urgent mandate to expand surge capacity under extreme volatility. This narrative explores the rapid transition of a Nursing Research and Innovation Director from strategic oversight to frontline clinical care within the Hospital at Home (HaH) framework. A primary element of this transition was the adaptation of clinical methods and resources to align with established, evidence-based safety standards in nontraditional care settings. The experience demonstrates that nursing leadership in conflict zones is most effective when it bridges the gap between high-level innovation and ground-level execution. By emphasizing clinical presence and agile operational management, this model ensures that acute care remains safe, standardized, and patient centered, even under active threat.

articles.title: Trends and Disparities in Pediatric Ophthalmologic Emergency Department Visits in New Jersey, 2020-2024: A 5-Year Population-Based Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: This study evaluated the volume, trends, and demographic disparities in pediatric ophthalmologic emergency department (ED) visits in New Jersey (NJ) from 2020 to 2024.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cross-sectional study used aggregate data from the NJ State Health Assessment Data (NJSHAD). We identified ED encounters among patients aged 0 to 19 years with primary ophthalmic ICD-10-CM diagnoses (H10, H00-H01, S05, H57.1, and T15). Temporal patterns were assessed using Pearson correlation and linear regression, with 2016 to 2019 used as a prepandemic reference. Demographic, payer, racial/ethnic rate, county, and workforce analyses were restricted to the 2020 to 2024 period.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 88,271 ophthalmologic ED encounters were included from 2016 to 2024. Annual volume averaged 12,095 encounters during 2016 to 2019 and fell to 4607 in 2020, 61.9% below the prepandemic mean. Visits subsequently recovered, although 2024 volume remained 15.2% below the 2016 to 2019 mean. Conjunctivitis remained near 30% of its prepandemic mean in 2020 to 2021, while traumatic diagnoses recovered from 51.4% to 71.0%. During 2020 to 2024, 39,890 encounters accounted for 1.37% of pediatric ED visits; Medicaid was the primary payer in 52.1% of cases. Conjunctivitis visit rates were 7.78 times higher among Black non-Hispanic children and 5.13 times higher among Hispanic children than among White non-Hispanic children. County rates correlated with Medicaid enrollment (r=0.861, P<0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Pediatric ophthalmologic ED visits in NJ fell sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequently recovered toward prepandemic levels. Higher conjunctivitis encounter rates among Black non-Hispanic and Hispanic children and in counties with greater Medicaid enrollment suggest persistent disparities in access to outpatient eye care.

articles.title: Circadian and Seasonal Patterns of Recorded Emergency Medical Service Workload by Diagnostic Category: A Two-Year Retrospective Analysis with Forecasting from Türkiye.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) demand varies across circadian, weekly, and seasonal timescales. This study is among the first such integrated analyses in the Turkish 112 EMS context.

abstract.label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The primary objective of this study was to characterize circadian patterns in overall EMS case-record volume and across seven clinical groups, as well as hourly, weekly, and seasonal variation in diagnostic composition across eight categories. Secondary objectives were to estimate adjusted temporal associations and evaluate frozen transfer of aggregate daily forecasts from 2024 to the immediately subsequent 2025 holdout.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective study analyzed 60,811 routinely collected EMS case-record rows from Karaman Province, Türkiye over 731 days in 2024-2025. Interaction, cosinor, and negative binomial (NB) models characterized temporal patterns; aggregate daily case-record volume was forecast using weekly Fourier terms with autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) errors trained on 2024 and frozen for 2025. The data represented provincial case-record workload, an operational proxy for population demand rather than a census of all inbound calls or unique patients.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Case-record volume peaked at 21:00 and was lowest at 06:00; adjusted volume at 21:00 was 3.53-times that at 06:00 (95% CI, 3.28-3.81). Hourly diagnostic composition differed modestly (Cramér V = 0.061). Rhythmicity was detected in all seven clinical groups (all joint-test P values < 0.001), but low full-cell R2 values indicated substantial unexplained hour-date variation; acrophases ranged from 14:41 to 19:14 and relative amplitudes from 28.6% (Respiratory) to 67.9% (Trauma). Standardized Trauma share was higher in summer than winter (25.7% versus 18.1%), whereas Respiratory share was higher in winter than summer (9.7% versus 3.6%). Adjusted volume was higher on Monday than Saturday and higher in August than November (IRRs 1.11 and 1.23, respectively). In the frozen 2025 holdout, the selected model achieved mean absolute scaled error (MASE) = 0.722 and 95% prediction-interval coverage of 96.2%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Clinical-group rhythms and seasonal composition differences were observed. The frozen evaluation quantified aggregate daily forecast transfer only from 2024 to the immediately subsequent 2025 within one provincial series. Findings support local monitoring of recorded evening workload and seasonal diagnostic composition, particularly the higher Trauma share in summer and the higher Respiratory share in winter.

articles.title: Real-World Health Care Resource Utilization, Adherence, and Persistence Following Subcutaneous IgPro20 Initiation Among US Patients with Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is a rare, inflammatory peripheral nervous system disorder. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been the standard maintenance therapy, but since 2018, Immune Globulin Subcutaneous (Human), 20% liquid (IgPro20), a subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) therapy, has offered an alternative, demonstrating benefit in maintaining CIDP improvement and remission. This study aimed to evaluate real-world healthcare resource utilization (HCRU), adherence, and persistence following IgPro20 initiation in patients with CIDP, given limited real-world evidence on these SCIG-related outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This observational, descriptive study used Optum's de-identified Clinformatics® Data Mart Database (Optum® CDM) data to examine adults with CIDP initiating IgPro20 (index date). Adult patients with ≥ 2 CIDP diagnosis claims at least 14 days apart and ≥ 6 months of enrollment pre- and post-index between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2024 were included. Those on other SCIG products were excluded.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Patients with CIDP initiating IgPro20 (N = 207) were 53.6% male, with a median age of 60.00 and few comorbidities. Acute care utilization was low at baseline and decreased further following IgPro20 initiation, with inpatient and emergency department visits per patient per year (PPPY) decreasing from 0.52 to 0.42 and from 1.00 to 0.85, respectively. Overall, outpatient (OP) visits increased from 60.62 PPPY pre-initiation to 92.61 PPPY in month 1 post-initiation, driven by visits for CIDP-related home administration, notably for nursing/home-care for self-administration training. OP visits subsequently declined to 67.43 PPPY by month 6 (n = 141). Most patients (69.1%) were highly adherent, and 63.8% remained persistent at 6 months.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Patients on IgPro20 administration demonstrated therapy adherence and decreased utilization of resource-intensive settings. While initial increases in outpatient and home care visits likely reflect training for at-home therapy, other outpatient healthcare utilization decreased. High persistence and adherence indicate sustained, uninterrupted therapy.

articles.title: Recurrent cardiac tamponade in a young man unmasking an endocrine surprise: a case record.
Development and validation of predictive models for undiagnosed Alzheimer's disease and related dementias in the emergency department.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The electronic health record (EHR) offers a promising resource to improve recognition of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), yet existing approaches have been developed within cohorts that underrepresent individuals prone to underdiagnosis and do not differentiate disease severity.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We applied a validated computational phenotype to identify probable ADRD (p-ADRD) and its severity within a random sample of 5000 individuals aged ≥65 years who presented to one of nine emergency departments in the Yale New Haven Health System (2014 to 2022). The dichotomous outcome was undiagnosed ADRD, assigned to those meeting criteria for p-ADRD but lacking validated diagnostic codes. We applied logistic regression with elastic net regularization to predict undiagnosed status for the overall cohort and within each severity stratum, assessing performance using 10-fold cross-validation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 1358 individuals with p-ADRD (mean age 86.7 years, standard deviation 7.4), 934 (68.8%) were undiagnosed. The overall model discriminated undiagnosed ADRD with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.85 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.83 to 0.87). The severity-stratified models achieved AUROC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.83) for mild and 0.91 (95% CI 0.88 to 0.94) for moderate to severe disease. Although the predictors of undiagnosed status differed by severity, fall-related injury was protective against underdiagnosis within each stratum.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: We developed and validated predictive models using structured EHR elements, which demonstrated robust discrimination of undiagnosed ADRD within a clinical cohort prone to underdiagnosis. The heterogeneous predictors across severity strata underscore the importance of aligning prediction with disease severity, given the distinct clinical needs that attend ADRD progression.

articles.title: Increased Prevalence of Large Language Model-Associated Language in US Residency Application Personal Statements.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Residency leaders increasingly rely on personal statements to assess applicant communication skills and individuality. Personal statements written by large language models (LLMs) have been rated more readable but more generic than applicant-written ones, yet the prevalence of LLM use and its effect on applicant writing remain unknown.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To measure the prevalence of LLM-associated language in personal statements from the 2017 through 2024 application cycles and assess associated changes in applicant writing.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective descriptive study analyzed personal statements submitted to the internal medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, emergency medicine, and general surgery residencies of a US academic medical center for the 2017 through 2024 application cycles. Using one-sample t tests, prevalence in 2024 of 27 LLM-associated words and 12 control words, identified in prior research, was compared to 2017-2023, the period before widespread LLM release. Secondary outcomes assessing writing characteristics reflective of communication skills and individuality included linguistic complexity (Flesch Reading Ease, word count), lexical diversity (type-token ratio), personalization (first- and third-person pronoun frequency), and topic entropy.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 62 132 statements (55 199 from 2017-2023, 6933 from 2024), LLM-associated word prevalence increased from 27.9% (SD, 1.05%) pre-2024 to 45.6% in 2024 (P<.001). Average length decreased from 717.2 (SD, 13.6) words to 676.6 (P<.001), while the type-token ratio increased from 0.49 (SD, 0.006) to 0.51 (P<.001). Approximately 3 fewer first-person pronouns were used per statement (P<.001). Topic entropy remained stable.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: LLM-associated language increased 17.7% in 2024, corresponding to approximately 1 in 6 additional personal statements, while writing characteristics reflective of communication skills and individuality changed modestly.

articles.title: Penetrating renal trauma in a high-complexity Latin American centre: Management patterns and renal preservation, 2013-2025 - a retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Contemporary renal-trauma practice rests on blunt-predominant cohorts from high-income trauma systems, and penetrating renal injury remains under-described. We characterised the management and outcomes of penetrating renal trauma at a high-complexity Latin American centre, with blunt injury as internal comparator, and examined how practice changed over 13 years.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort of 161 consecutive adults (≥18 years) treated between February 2013 and July 2025, classified by mechanism. Management, nephrectomy and in-hospital outcomes are reported descriptively as n (%) and median [IQR]. Testing was confined to three pre-specified questions: whether nephrectomy differed by mechanism; whether it differed by mechanism among patients taken to open surgery; and whether it changed over time. Two-sided exact p values were obtained by doubling the one-sided probability.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty-four injuries (21%) were penetrating (27 gunshot, 6 stab, 1 unspecified) and 126 (78%) blunt. Among penetrating injuries, 13 (38%) were managed non-operatively, 3 (9%) with angioembolisation and 18 (53%) with open surgery. Non-operative management was used up to AAST grade IV and failed in none, with no reintervention, nephrectomy or renal complication; angioembolisation preserved every treated kidney. Twelve of the 34 penetrating injuries (35%) ended in nephrectomy versus 5 of 126 blunt (4%; p < 0.001), and every nephrectomy in the cohort followed open surgery. Among the patients taken to open surgery, however, nephrectomy was equally frequent in the two groups (12 of 18 vs 5 of 9; p = 0.88), so renal loss tracked the decision to operate rather than intraoperative salvageability. High-grade (AAST IV-V) injury was similarly frequent by mechanism (41% vs 29%). Within penetrating injuries, open surgery fell from 15 of 24 in 2013-2019-3 of 10 in 2020-2025, and nephrectomy from 11 of 24-1 of 10, with a stable mechanism mix.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Selective non-operative management and angioembolisation preserved every kidney in which they were used, including after penetrating injury, and renal loss followed the decision to operate rather than the mechanism itself. These data support extending physiology-guided, kidney-preserving management to penetrating renal injury.

articles.title: Contemporary Approaches to Prehospital Acute Coronary Syndrome Risk Stratification: A Narrative Review.

abstract.text: Chest pain is a common high-risk complaint encountered by emergency medical services (EMS). Early identification and treatment of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) improve outcomes, yet prehospital evaluation remains constrained by limited diagnostic resources. This narrative review examines contemporary approaches to prehospital ACS risk stratification, diagnostic technologies, and decision-making. A targeted PubMed search of peer-reviewed publications and selected grey literature published between 2020 and 2025 was supplemented by targeted searches and citation review. Relevant literature published after the initial search period was incorporated during manuscript preparation and revision. Studies addressing prehospital ACS risk stratification, electrocardiogram (ECG) assessment, point-ofcare biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted diagnostics, and systems-level cardiac triage were included and synthesized thematically. Biomarker-integrated pathways, particularly HEART-derived approaches combined with point-of-care troponin testing, demonstrated the strongest evidence for safe prehospital risk assessment and reduced healthcare utilization. Biomarker-free approaches offered broader applicability but lower diagnostic certainty. ECG acquisition and transmission remained foundational for STEMI recognition and activation, while AI-assisted ECG interpretation and decision-support tools showed promising diagnostic performance but lacked prospective outcome-based validation. Gaps remain regarding atypical presentations, sex-specific strategies, and validation across diverse EMS environments. Overall, contemporary evidence supports structured prehospital risk stratification as decision support rather than definitive diagnosis. Implementation depends on provider training, protocol standardization, resources, and integration within regional systems of care. Future research should prioritize validation across diverse EMS settings, atypical and sex-specific presentations, and prospective evaluation of emerging diagnostic technologies.

articles.title: Beyond Parametric and Nonparametric Tests: A Practical Guide to Table 1 in Clinical Research.

abstract.text: In many clinical research reports, Table 1 presents the baseline or general characteristics of study participants and helps readers understand the study population and observed between-group differences. Despite its apparent simplicity, constructing and interpreting Table 1 requires several distinct decisions, including whether formal between-group inference is scientifically justified, how variables should be summarized, and how observed differences should be interpreted. Routine significance testing of baseline characteristics is generally discouraged in randomized trials and often provides limited information in observational studies, where group differences may reflect treatment selection, exposure patterns, disease severity, or other systematic mechanisms. We propose a purpose-first framework in which investigators first clarify the intended role of Table 1, consider the study design, and determine whether a comparison addresses a prespecified and scientifically meaningful inferential question. They should then identify the variable type, evaluate distributional shape, influential observations, and clinical interpretability, and select appropriate summary statistics. For descriptive applications, transparent group-specific summaries should be emphasized, with observed absolute or standardized differences added when useful and without routine p-values. Confidence intervals should be reported when a population-level estimation objective has been defined. When formal inference is justified, investigators should define the target quantity or estimand and select a statistical method according to the variable type, data structure, distributional characteristics, and model assumptions. Effect estimates and confidence intervals should receive greater emphasis than isolated p-values. This framework distinguishes description from inference and promotes transparent, statistically coherent, and clinically meaningful construction and interpretation of Table 1.

articles.title: Large Language Models in the Emergency Department: Fairness Implications for Clinicians.

abstract.text: Applications of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are rapidly expanding in emergency medicine, but concerns remain regarding their fairness across diverse patient populations. Fairness extends beyond model accuracy and includes equal performance across patient groups, equitable outcomes and allocation of clinical benefits, and procedural fairness throughout the lifecycle of AI implementation. This narrative review aims to provide a practical framework for understanding and evaluating fairness in emergency medicine applications of AI and LLMs. This narrative review organizes fairness risks into three clinically relevant layers. First, datalevel fairness concerns the data used to train, fine-tune, or prompt AI systems. Biased clinical data, including non-random missingness and stigmatizing documentation, can influence model performance. Second, output-level fairness concerns whether the outputs generated by AI systems are equally accurate, safe, and useful across patient groups. In emergency care, subgroup-specific errors in recommendations, predictions, translations, or instructions may arise from aggregation, learning, or evaluation bias, even when overall model performance appears strong. Third, human-interaction fairness concerns whether the benefits of AI are realized equitably in clinical practice and by patients. Even when data and outputs are fair, inequities may arise if clinicians over-rely on or reject useful AI recommendations, or if patients are unable to access, understand, or trust AI-mediated information. Clinicians should consider potential implications for safety, transparency, and fairness alongside overall model accuracy when evaluating AI tools in emergency medicine.

articles.title: Propensity score methods in medical research: a concise practical guide with applications to emergency medicine.

abstract.text: Propensity score (PS) methods can reduce measured confounding in observational emergency medicine research, but validity depends more on design choices and diagnostics than on the treatment-prediction model. This clinical review presents a practical workflow for defining the target estimand, selecting pretreatment covariates, choosing matching or weighting, checking covariate balance and treatment overlap, and analyzing a binary outcome in the population created by the PS design. The average treatment effect (ATE), average treatment effect in the treated (ATT), and average treatment effect in the overlap population (ATO) answer different clinical questions. A worked example of 1,200 simulated emergency patients uses a common, explicit time zero to show how confounding by indication can make immediate treatment appear harmful before adjustment and how PS matching, stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting, and overlap weighting change both the comparison population and estimated effect. Standardized mean differences, PS distributions, weight summaries, and effective sample size are presented before treatment-specific risks, risk differences, and risk ratios. A standalone supplement provides package-based R code, expected output, and analysis-derived figures. Survival analysis is outside the scope. PS methods are most credible when used as design tools: define the question, construct a supported comparison, verify diagnostics, and only then analyze outcomes.

articles.title: Hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices after cardiac arrest: a cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from higher hemoglobin targets. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. We screened in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests with resuscitation efforts ongoing at hospital arrival for inclusion. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Exploratory analyses evaluated the association between hemoglobin and in-hospital mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post-arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,238 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). Pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels were < 7 g/dL for 762 (61.6%) of transfusions, and ≥ 7 g/dL for 476 (38.4%) of transfusions. Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 h. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation in pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.

articles.title: Work productivity and psychological well-being in patients affected by type 1 diabetes mellitus.

abstract.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) is a lifelong autoimmune condition that, when diagnosed during childhood or adolescence, may influence educational attainment, employment trajectories, and occupational functioning in adulthood. This observational cross-sectional study, conducted between June and September 2024 at the "Federico II" University Hospital in Naples, Italy, assessed work ability, work productivity, activity impairment, and psychological well-being in 70 adults with T1D. Sociodemographic, clinical, and occupational data were collected through structured interviews and medical record review. Work ability was evaluated using the Work Ability Index (WAI), productivity and activity impairment using the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire (WPAI), and psychological well-being using the Psychological General Well-Being Index (PGWBI). Overall, 49% of participants were unemployed. Among employed individuals, work ability was generally preserved, with 72% reporting good or excellent WAI scores, although WAI declined significantly with age (p = 0.040). WPAI results showed low absenteeism (5.5%) but relevant presenteeism (26.7%) and activity impairment (42.7%). Activity impairment was higher among unemployed than employed participants (61.2% vs. 25.3%; p < 0.0001). Mean PGWBI scores indicated preserved psychological well-being (66.8 ± 20.3) but declined with increasing age (p = 0.001) and unemployment (p = 0.003). Higher PGWBI scores correlated with greater work ability (rs = 0.72, p < 0.0001) and lower activity impairment (rs = -0.79, p < 0.0001). Glycated hemoglobin, body mass index, occupational category, and insulin delivery technology were not significantly associated with outcomes. Overall, age and employment status emerged as relevant correlates of functional and psychological outcomes. These findings support integrated occupational strategies beyond glycemic control and appropriate targeted workplace accommodations.

articles.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Synthesis of Qualitative Studies on Women's Experiences of Initial Miscarriage Care at the First Point of Clinical Contact.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Miscarriage is a common pregnancy complication, yet women's experiences of care at the first point of clinical contact remain insufficiently understood. This systematic review and qualitative meta-synthesis examined how women experience and evaluate initial miscarriage care and what needs and priorities they identify during this early stage.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: CINAHL, Scopus, and PubMed were systematically searched for qualitative and mixed methods studies published between January 2015 and December 2024 following a preregistered protocol on the Open Science Framework and PRISMA 2020 guidance.

abstract.label: STUDY SELECTION
abstract.text: Eligibility criteria were developed using the SPIDER framework and included studies reporting women's experiences of care at first clinical contact for miscarriage (e.g., emergency departments, early pregnancy assessment units, outpatient triage) and published in English. Of 1,091 records identified (1,035 after deduplication), 45 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 10 studies, predominantly from high-income settings, met the inclusion criteria. Studies were appraised for methodological quality using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist.

abstract.label: DATA EXTRACTION
abstract.text: Data relevant to women's experiences, needs, and priorities during early miscarriage care were extracted from the 10 studies involving 232 women (nurses and nurse managers interviewed alongside parents in one review were not counted, consistent with this review's inclusion criteria) and synthesized thematically.

abstract.label: DATA SYNTHESIS
abstract.text: Four themes were developed: Emotional Shock and Vulnerability, Communication and Information Gaps, Clinical Prioritization Versus Emotional Needs, and Navigating Discharge and Ongoing Uncertainty. Across studies, initial miscarriage services were found to prioritize physical management while frequently overlooking emotional and informational support.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This review offers a focused synthesis of women's experiences at the earliest stages of miscarriage care, revealing a persistent gap between clinical and emotional responsiveness. The findings provide new evidence to inform more compassionate, woman-centered early miscarriage pathways that integrate timely clinical care with clear communication and psychosocial support.

articles.title: Can frailty screening be used to inform clinical decision-making for older persons in the emergency department? A systematic review.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Older adults with frailty presenting to the emergency department (ED) have worse short- and long-term outcomes than those who are not frail. Frailty screenings are often applied retrospectively to demonstrate a relationship between frailty and outcomes; it is not known whether frailty screening can inform decision-making about acuity at triage or ED disposition.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To determine whether the use of frailty screening at triage or during an ED stay can inform triage acuity or provide information to inform disposition decisions.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Covidence software was used to identify primary studies conducted from 2000-present with a patient population of greater than 65 years of age, presenting to the ED, which described using a frailty tool to inform clinical decision-making. Exclusion criteria comprised case reports, systematic reviews, conference abstracts, non-ED settings, written in a language other than English, or in which frailty was used as a covariant rather than a predictor. The search yielded 6360 studies for screening. 2042 duplicates were identified and removed. Of the 4318 remaining abstracts screened, 93 full-text studies met initial criteria and were assessed for eligibility, and 88 of them were excluded. Five studies were evaluated for this review.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Early identification of frailty at triage facilitates intervention by case management or geriatric-specific care teams which can reduce ED under-triage, ED revisits, and re-admission in patients greater than 65 years of age who screen positive for frailty.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Frailty screening processes can and should be used to identify older patients who may be more acutely ill than they initially appear at presentation, or may require more consideration at the point of discharge decision-making and may benefit from medical or case management interventions in the ED.

articles.title: Current Evidence of Minimizing Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in a Rat Flap Model: A Systematic Review.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: To reduce the risk of ischemia-reperfusion injury following free tissue transfer, many treatments focus on the upregulation of the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory responses to promote reversible cell injury by reducing oxygen free radicals, mitochondrial damage, neutrophil-mediated inflammation, and complement activation. This review aims to characterize interventions in rats for reducing flap necrosis as a result of ischemia-reperfusion injury.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Following the 2020 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic review of the PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and OVID repositories was conducted from inception to July 2025. The inclusion criteria consisted of any study focusing on minimizing ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat flap models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 2448 unique citations, 72 (n = 3423 rats) were included. Interventions included pharmacological therapies (n = 54/72, 75%), followed by surgical (n = 12/72, 16.7%), hyperbaric oxygen (n = 4/72, 5.6%), biological (n = 3/72, 4.2%), temperature (n = 1/72, 1.4%), and perfusion (n = 1/72, 1.4%) therapies. The overall success rate of interventions for minimizing ischemia-reperfusion injury was 97.2% (n = 70/72). Of the 56 unique interventions identified, further research involving large animal models was conducted in 9/56 (16.1%), whereas human involvement was reported in 6/56 (10.7%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Interventions demonstrated a high reported rate of success for reducing ischemia-reperfusion injury (97.2%). However, only 10.7% of interventions were found to be further studied among human patients, highlighting the need for additional research to reduce ischemia-reperfusion injury without significant disruptions to the perioperative workflow. Identification of the patient population that would benefit most from prophylactic interventions is also needed.

articles.title: Immobilized Neuroglobin Scavenges Carbon Monoxide From Circulating Carboxyhemoglobin.
articles.journal_full: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)

abstract.text: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is responsible for around 50,000 emergency department visits per year in the United States alone. Currently, there is no available antidote for CO poisoning. We have previously developed an antidotal therapy based on an engineered hemeprotein, human neuroglobin (Ngb-H64Q-CCC). Intravenous infusion of Ngb-H64Q-CCC removes CO from circulating red blood cells and improves survival in a lethal CO poisoning mouse model. However, the infusion of heme-containing proteins has inherent heme toxicity risks that may limit the dose that can be used safely without liver or kidney toxicity. To overcome these problems, we have investigated the development of immobilized Ngb in a solid matrix. This approach allows for the development of a CO removal system using an extracorporeal blood-circulating system coupled with a stationary matrix with immobilized Ngb-H64Q-CCC. Such a system avoids drug infusion and possible organ injury, allows for antidote recycling, and provides advantages for storage and handling of the antidote. Here we have developed Ngb-H64Q-CCC covalently bound to N-hydroxysuccinimide agarose. The immobilized protein shows preserved heme redox activity and retains its CO removal capacity after successive regeneration cycles. We expect that this novel approach will advance the development of new scavenger-based therapies for CO poisoning.

articles.title: Authors' reply: Comment on "trauma-specific revision of the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine disseminated intravascular coagulation criteria improves outcome prediction in severely injured patients".
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
authors: Japanese Observational Study for Coagulation and Thrombolysis in Early Trauma 2 (J-OCTET2) investigators

articles.title: Beyond the destination: Transfer time and pediatric specialization in severe traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

articles.title: Multicompartmental hemorrhage: A high-risk pattern associated with increased risk for progression in TBI patients.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) often requires repeat head computed tomography (CT) imaging to monitor for bleed progression. While prior literature has explored patient-level factors, data on the impact of ICH morphologies (subdural [SDH], epidural [EDH], intraparenchymal [IPH], intraventricular [IVH], and multicompartment hemorrhage [MCH]) on radiographic ICH progression remains unclear. We hypothesized that MCH and IVH would have an increased associated risk of progression.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective (2021-2023) single-center cohort included adults (≥18 y) with TBI-related ICH who underwent initial and repeat head CT. Patients were stratified into radiographic progression versus no-progression cohorts, with progression defined as new or enlarging hemorrhage on attending radiologist interpretation of follow-up head CT. The primary outcome was the rate of radiographic progression for each ICH type. MCH was defined as the presence of two or more ICH types. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between each ICH type and radiographic progression, adjusting for age, mechanism of injury, Injury Severity Score, Glasgow Coma Scale on arrival, trauma-bay intubation, and preinjury antithrombotic exposure.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 817 patients with ICH on initial head CT and documented repeat CT, 401 (49.1%) had radiographic progression. Patients with progression were younger (58 vs. 62 y, p=0.027), more frequently male (71.3% vs. 63.7%, p=0.020), and had similar antithrombotic exposure (15.2% vs. 14.2%, p=0.678). Craniotomy/craniectomy was more frequent among those with progression (21.2% vs. 8.2%, p<0.001). On multivariable analysis, MCH demonstrated the strongest associated risk for progression (odds ratio [OR] 5.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.36-9.33, p<0.001), whereas IPH (OR 2.02, CI: 0.86-4.75, p=0.108), SDH, EDH, and IVH were not independently associated with radiographic ICH progression.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: MCH was independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. This higher-risk hemorrhage pattern may warrant closer neurological monitoring.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Prognostic/Epidemiologic; Level III.

articles.title: A clinically relevant porcine model of flail chest: Development and multimodal validation.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Flail chest has high mortality, but large-animal models with thoracic anatomy comparable to humans are lacking. The objective of this study was to develop a clinically relevant porcine flail chest model that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, and to validate it using multimodal assessment including computed tomography (CT) imaging and physiologic parameters.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Twelve male Landrace pigs were randomly assigned to a flail chest (FC) group and a multiple single rib fracture (MRF) group (n=6 per group). Under general anesthesia, controlled osteotomies were performed on the fifth to eighth ribs.
