Higher insomnia severity was observed among single students than among married students (12.1 vs. 7.4, p = 0.005), among students at private universities (19.3 vs. 11.6, p = 0.001), and among those with chronic medical or diagnosed mental illness (p < 0.05). No significant differences were found by gender, region, academic level, or dormitory residence (p > 0.05). Regression analysis showed that marital status and university type were significant predictors of insomnia symptom severity. Conclusions: Insomnia is common among EMS students and may have implications for both student well-being and future clinical performance. Addressing sleep health within EMS education may support better academic outcomes and safer healthcare delivery.

articles.title: Recent advances in pediatric pulmonology: Articles of interest to fellows. Azithromycin for preschool wheezing, combined maternal RSV immunization and infant nirsevimab, and oscillometric assessment of small-airway dysfunction.

abstract.text: Recent advances in pediatric respiratory medicine continue to refine preventive strategies, therapeutic decision-making, and physiological assessment. This review highlights three recent publications of particular interest to pediatric pulmonology fellows. First, we discuss a multicenter randomized trial demonstrating that azithromycin does not improve outcomes in preschool children presenting to the emergency department with moderate-to-severe wheezing, despite effectively eradicating respiratory bacterial colonization. Second, we review an interim randomized trial showing that combined maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccination and infant nirsevimab appear safe and elicit robust antibody responses, with no evidence of immune interference. Finally, we summarize evidence that impulse oscillometry can detect subclinical small-airway dysfunction in children with well-controlled asthma despite normal spirometry. Together, these studies highlight the growing importance of evidence-based prevention, antimicrobial stewardship, and precision respiratory assessment in pediatric practice.

articles.title: Integrating emergency medical services and hospital surge capacity for mass-gathering preparedness: a structured narrative review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Mass gatherings can generate concentrated, time-dependent demand across in-event health services, municipal emergency medical services (EMS), emergency departments, and inpatient services. Evidence relevant to preparedness is heterogeneous and is often reported with inconsistent denominators, limiting direct comparison.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This structured narrative review synthesizes published evidence on EMS and hospital surge-capacity integration across the four surge domains of staff, stuff/supplies, space, and systems. The review retained the original structured search of MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for 2010-February 2026 and incorporated a focused PubMed and citation update through September 2026. Because the purpose is interpretive synthesis rather than exhaustive effect estimation, no de novo meta-analysis or pooled estimates were produced; quantitative findings are reported with the denominators and analytic context used by the source publications.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A 2025 scoping review of 41 papers reported medical-doctor presence in 34/41 papers (82.9%), medication interventions in 23/41 (56.1%), procedural interventions in 23/41 (56.1%), health-support systems in 18/41 (43.9%), mobile treatment spaces in 23/41 (56.1%), and temporary structures in 21/41 (51.2%). That review reported median calculated patient-presentation and transport-to-hospital rates of 6.2 and 0.35 per 1,000 attendees, respectively, whereas a separate 22-article stadium review reported much lower medians when standardized per 10,000 spectators. Hospital effects were directionally heterogeneous: a 14-study systematic review found event-associated emergency-department changes ranging from 7.5%-37% decreases to increases as high as 83% in specific settings. Digital integration has shown promising simulated gains, but clinical effectiveness remains insufficiently validated.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Preparedness is best treated as an integrated continuum rather than as separate event-site and hospital plans. Standardized denominators, linked patient-level data, context-specific resource design, and prospective evaluation are priorities.

articles.title: When diabetic ketoacidosis becomes a neurological emergency: cerebral edema in a child with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus - a case report and narrative review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D), potentially leading to severe outcomes, including cerebral edema (CE). The case describes an eight-year-old child with previously undiagnosed T1D complicated by DKA, and subsequent development of CE. It is followed by a short literature review including other pediatric cases of clinically overt CE.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A boy was admitted to the outpatient clinic with a several-day history of vomiting, abdominal pain and headache, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of gastrointestinal infection. The following day, the patient's condition deteriorated. Despite a positive family history of T1D (the patient's father), his blood glucose level was measured for the first time by the emergency medical service (25.6 mmol/L (460 mg/dL)). Further evaluation revealed DKA secondary to previously undiagnosed T1D. On admission, the boy was in severe general condition. Severe DKA was confirmed (pH 6.88), and appropriate treatment was implemented, resulting in temporary clinical stabilization. However, on the second day of hospitalization, the patient's condition deteriorated again. He was somnolent, with fluctuating consciousness and nuchal rigidity. An increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) was suspected. Optic nerve ultrasonography revealed increased optic nerve sheath diameters, also suggestive of raised ICP. Anti-edema therapy with mannitol was initiated based on clinical suspicion, resulting in clinical improvement. Dexamethasone and furosemide were administered as adjunctive therapy. Subsequent CT findings supported the diagnosis of CE. The patient was discharged after 10 days in good general condition.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: DKA can be a diagnostic challenge for clinicians due to its nonspecific symptoms. Early signs suggesting this condition should not be underestimated, and bedside blood glucose should be measured early in children presenting with unexplained vomiting, weight loss, tachypnea, dehydration or altered consciousness. Close monitoring for complications is critical during treatment, especially for CE, one of the most serious and potentially life-threatening consequences of DKA.

articles.title: Comparison of Ultrasound and Computed Tomography Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter for Intracranial Pressure Assessment in Pediatric Neurocritical Care.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Noninvasive intracranial pressure (ICP) assessment remains challenging in pediatric neurocritical care. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured by ultrasound (ONSD-US) and computed tomography (ONSD-CT) has been proposed as a surrogate marker of ICP, although comparative pediatric data remain limited.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Prospective observational study conducted in a tertiary pediatric intensive care unit. Patients requiring invasive ICP monitoring were consecutively included. ONSD-US measurements were obtained simultaneously with invasive ICP measurements and, for patients undergoing CT, within 5 minutes before or after transfer for imaging. Pearson correlation and linear mixed-effects models accounting for repeated measurements were used. Bland-Altman analysis assessed intermodality agreement.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eighteen patients contributed 139 measurement occasions. ONSD-US measurements were available in 116 occasions and ONSD-CT measurements in 37; 14 paired measurements from 11 patients included both modalities. One additional CT-derived measurement was excluded because of inadequate image quality, while the corresponding ONSD-US measurement was retained. ONSD-US showed a positive correlation with ICP (r = 0.32, P < 0.001), whereas ONSD-CT did not demonstrate a significant correlation (r = 0.23, P = 0.17). In mixed-effects analysis, each 1-mm increase in ONSD-US was associated with an estimated 3.24-mmHg increase in ICP (standard error 1.10; 95% confidence interval 1.09-5.39). Correlation between modalities was weak and not statistically significant (r = 0.31, P = 0.29).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: ONSD-US demonstrated an association with invasively measured ICP after accounting for repeated measurements, whereas ONSD-CT did not show a clear association. Weak intermodality correlation suggests that ONSD-US and ONSD-CT should not be considered interchangeable methods for noninvasive ICP assessment in pediatric neurocritical care.

articles.title: Perceived Social and Emotional Support from Co-Workers and Supervisors and Occupational Stress in Emergency Physicians: A Pre-Pandemic National Cross-Sectional Study from Slovenia.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Emergency physicians report high levels of occupational stress, but its organisational determinants remain under-investigated, particularly in small national systems. This exploratory, pre-pandemic study examined occupational stress among emergency medicine specialists in Slovenia, hypothesising that lower perceived support from supervisors and from co-workers would be associated with greater stress. Methods: All 86 emergency medicine specialists registered in Slovenia were surveyed in March-April 2019, and 45 participated (52.3%). Stress and support were measured with the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire and analysed with correlation coefficients, t-tests and Mann-Whitney tests, with multivariable regression as a sensitivity analysis. Results: Support was perceived as lowest from supervisors and highest from partners, family and friends. Lower perceived supervisor support was associated with poor interpersonal relationships at work (r = 0.568), poor job fit, a poor work environment, lower job control and total stress (r = 0.488); lower co-worker support was only associated with poor job fit and work perceived as not worth doing. Neither was associated with the intrinsic demands of the work. After adjustment for sex, age and tenure, supervisor support (β = 0.49) and female sex (β = 0.34) remained independently associated with total stress (adjusted R2 = 0.30). Conclusions: The hypothesis was supported for supervisor support but only partly for co-worker support. The small sample, multiple comparisons and cross-sectional design make these findings exploratory and specific to the pre-pandemic period. As perceived support is organisationally modifiable, leadership and peer support are identified as targets for future intervention research, and multinational studies in comparable emergency systems are warranted.

articles.title: Is a Repeat Head CT Scan Necessary After an Initial Negative Scan in Head Trauma Patients on DOAC Therapy in the Emergency Department?

abstract.text: Background: Head trauma in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) presents a clinical dilemma because of concern for delayed intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). Although some emergency departments (EDs) routinely perform repeat head CT after an initially negative scan, the clinical value of this practice remains uncertain. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study at Hadassah Mount Scopus University Hospital Emergency Department (ED), a level 3 trauma center with approximately 70,000 visits per year, spanning January 2019 to December 2022. Adult patients receiving DOAC therapy who sustained blunt head trauma and underwent both an initial and repeat head CT according to institutional protocol were included. Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, type of DOAC, and CT findings were recorded. Exclusion criteria included: penetrating trauma, multi trauma, identified intracranial hemorrhage on the first scan, age < 18 years, and pregnancy status. Results: A total of 421 patients met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 80.1 years, and 236 patients (56%) were female. Apixaban was the most prescribed DOAC (364 patients, 86%), followed by rivaroxaban (39 patients, 9.5%) and dabigatran (18 patients, 4.5%). Glasgow Coma Scale was 15 in 399 patients (94.7%) on presentation. Five patients (1.2%,95% CI: 0.5-2.8%) had delayed ICH on repeat CT after an initially negative scan. All five patients were older than 75 years and had visible evidence of blunt head trauma, and one required neurosurgical intervention. Conclusions: Delayed ICH after blunt head trauma in DOAC-treated patients with an initially negative CT was uncommon. These findings support that routine repeat CT scanning for all patients may be unnecessary, and a more focused subsequent CT scan strategy could ultimately optimize hospital resources without compromising patient safety-specifically among elderly patients, those with a low GCS, or showing evidence of trauma. Future research should also evaluate whether emerging blood-based biomarkers can help identify DOAC-treated patients at risk for delayed intracranial hemorrhage despite an initially negative CT scan.

articles.title: Mechanism matters with traumatic rectal injuries: Multicenter analysis of blunt versus penetrating traumatic rectal injury management and associated outcomes.
authors: AAST Contemporary Management of Rectal Injuries Study Group

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Examine the impact of injury mechanism and management strategies on outcomes after traumatic rectal injury (TRI).

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: TRI are uncommon, with most data derived from penetrating injuries. Whether management and outcomes differ between blunt (BR) and penetrating (PR) injuries remains unclear.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A multicenter study across 22 trauma centers compared management patterns, use of the "4 Ds" adjuncts (drain, diversion, distal washout, direct repair), and outcomes between BR and PR.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 725 patients (511 PR, 214 BR), BR had higher injury severity, more abdominal complications, and required more interventions despite similar TRI grade. Mortality was lowest in PR managed with adjuncts and highest in BR without adjuncts. In BR, diversion-only management resulted in the highest complication and reintervention rates. Drain and distal washout were also associated with increased abdominal complications. Multivariable analysis showed diversion-only management independently increased complications versus primary repair.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: BR carry greater morbidity than PR and may favor repair strategies.

articles.title: Prehospital extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a protocol for the Rapid prehospital ACcess to ECPR in Prague (RACE Prague) single-arm pilot feasibility study.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is strongly time dependent, yet in established in-hospital ECPR systems, including Prague, the median collapse-to-flow time has remained around 60 min or more, dominated by intra-arrest transport. Evidence for prehospital ECPR remains limited, particularly its comparison with in-hospital ECPR. RACE Prague evaluates whether dispatching a mobile cannulation team to the scene shortens this interval within the same ECPR system.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Single-centre, prospective, interventional, single-arm pilot feasibility study. Twenty adults aged 18-70 years with witnessed refractory OHCA (three unsuccessful defibrillations and/or ≥10 min of resuscitation in pulseless electrical activity), receive prehospital percutaneous femoro-femoral veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) from a mobile ECPR team. The primary endpoint (time from estimated collapse to ECMO flow ≥2.0 L/min) is tested hierarchically against the historical Prague OHCA in-hospital ECPR cohort (target shortening ≥15 min) and a contemporaneous in-hospital ECPR cohort at the same centre. Secondary endpoints include 30-day survival with favourable neurological outcome assessed blind, decomposition of prehospital pathway intervals, cannulation success, and pre-specified safety endpoints. Enrolment proceeds without prior consent under ethics-approved emergency-research provisions, with deferred consent thereafter.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: RACE Prague is testing the effect of cannulation location on the time to extracorporeal support and will provide essential evidence on the feasibility of prehospital ECPR.Trial registration:ClinicalTrials.govNCT06789978; Ethics Committee of the General University Hospital in Prague, reference 134/23 S-IV.

articles.title: Health system readiness for out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest management in resource limited settings: A mixed-method study from rural and suburban Sindh, Pakistan.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest requires a robust emergency response system for survival. In low-resource settings like suburban and rural Sindh in Pakistan, little is known about the readiness of healthcare systems and communities.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to comprehensively assess the system-readiness for out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest management in rural and suburban areas of Sindh, Pakistan by studying out-of-hospital and in-hospital elements of chain of survival in these areas.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A triangulation mixed-methods design was used. The study was conducted in seven hospitals in the suburban and rural areas of upper, central and southern parts of the province of Sindh, Pakistan. Quantitative data from exit interviews (n = 163) using the Patient Satisfaction Questionnaire-18 and a facility readiness checklist (n = 7 hospitals) were analysed using descriptive statistics. Qualitative data were collected through focus group discussions with community members and ambulance crew, in-depth interviews with emergency room doctors and nurses, and key informant interviews with emergency room supervisors and cardiologists and were analysed using thematic analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Exit interviews with 163 patients showed that the lowest proportions satisfied were for communication (26.4%), financial aspects (31.3%), accessibility and convenience (32.5%), technical quality of emergency room staff (40.5%), and time spent with doctors (47.2%). Among the seven facilities assessed, defibrillators were available in two, but neither was functional; epinephrine was available in four, pulse oximeters in three, and endotracheal tubes in three, while laryngeal mask airways were unavailable in all facilities. Qualitative data from 12 focus group discussions, 15 in-depth interviews, and three key informant interviews identified limited recognition of cardiac arrest, inadequate ambulance availability, poor road access, shortages of trained staff and resuscitation equipment, sociocultural and gender-related barriers, and weaknesses in emergency care governance and data systems.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Triangulation of quantitative and qualitative findings showed that the Chain of Survival in rural and suburban Sindh is weak at several points, including the community, prehospital care, health facilities, and governance.The study shows that there is a need to strengthen the system at multiple levels. This includes training community members, ambulance crew and emergency room staff in cardiopulmonary resuscitation, setting minimum standards for resuscitation readiness, and creating out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest registries.

articles.title: Perceived factors influencing healthcare professionals' adherence to the ABCDE approach: an exploratory explanatory sequential mixed-methods study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure (ABCDE) approach is considered the preferred way to assess potentially critically ill patients. This study aimed to identify perceived factors influencing healthcare professionals' adherence to the ABCDE approach.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: An exploratory, explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was performed, comprising an cross-sectional questionnaire phase followed by semi-structured focus groups. A total of 239 healthcare professionals (nurses, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, residents and medical specialists) from six disciplines (Anaesthesiology, Emergency Medicine, Paediatrics and the Neonatal, Paediatric and Adult Intensive Care Units) filled out a questionnaire. Questionnaire results were analysed and used as input for five semi-structured focus groups with 22 participants. The focus groups were transcribed and analysed using template analysis, complemented by identification of additional themes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Perceived factors influencing adherence to the approach were categorised into five domains: guideline, individual health professional, patient, professional interactions, and incentives/resources. The importance of the ABCDE approach was affirmed, with 95.4% recognising it as their responsibility to perform the approach. Confidence in competency was high with a median rating of 90% (IQR 80-99) on a 0-100% scale. While feedback was considered valuable, 68.2% indicated it was provided rarely. Other identified factors included the ABCDE approach's simplicity and structure, healthcare professionals' experience, patient condition, the presence of a predefined team leader, and the role of regular education. 'Context dependency', 'ABCDE as a language' and 'Personal value' were identified as additional themes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This study identified perceived factors influencing healthcare professionals' adherence to the ABCDE approach. Adequate application of the ABCDE approach may require continuous learning in education and clinical practice.

articles.title: Neuroprotective effect of early remote ischaemic post-conditioning after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (RIPOST-CA): study protocol for a randomised, single-blinded, monocentric, controlled trial.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury is the leading cause of death and long-term disability after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and is driven by the ischaemia-reperfusion syndrome, for which no specific treatment exists. Remote ischaemic post-conditioning (brief, repeated cycles of limb ischaemia and reperfusion delivered with a pneumatic cuff), is protective across ischemia-reperfusion conditions. We aim to assess whether early conditioning reduces hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-centre, single-blinded, randomised (1:1) controlled trial with blinded assessment of the outcome, enrols 48 comatose adults resuscitated from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Participants receive standard post-resuscitation care with three sham cuff sessions, or standard care plus three sessions of conditioning (thigh cuff, four cycles of 5-min inflation at 200 mmHg alternating with 5-min deflation), the first within 4 h of return of spontaneous circulation and repeated at the 12th and 24th hour. Randomisation is stratified by initial rhythm (shockable versus non-shockable). The primary endpoint is the change in serum neurofilament light chain between the 6th and 72nd hour after return of spontaneous circulation. Secondary endpoints include daily Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores (days 1-3), serum neuron-specific enolase and protein S100-B kinetics, in-intensive care unit mortality by cause, and a favourable neurological outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0-3) at intensive care unit discharge and at 90 days.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: RIPOST-CA is the first randomised trial to evaluate early remote ischemic post-conditioning on brain-injury biomarkers after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Its results could inform larger clinical trials of this simple, non-invasive intervention.Trial registration number: NCT06473207.

articles.title: Emergency Department Overcrowding Despite Lower Post-Pandemic Volumes: A Multicenter Study.

abstract.text: Background: The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly affected emergency department (ED) activity worldwide, and health system constraints may persist beyond the pandemic phase. Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included all ED visits by patients aged ≥14 years at four Italian tertiary EDs in 2019 and 2024. Input, throughput, and output measures were compared using negative binomial regression and Weibull accelerated failure time models. Results: Overall, 286,298 visits occurred in 2024 and 310,900 in 2019 (adjusted change, -5.5%; 95% CI -9.8 to -1.0). The reduction mainly involved low-priority and daytime presentations. Despite lower input, flow metrics and crowding worsened. Door-to-physician time increased from 51 to 58 min (+21.6%; 95% CI 20.9 to 22.4). Median ED occupancy increased by 8.0% (95% CI 4.5 to 11.6), and the number of patients who left without being seen (LWBS) increased by 17.1% (95% CI 12.9 to 21.5). Total ED LOS increased from 3 h 48 min to 4 h 27 min (+15.1%; 95% CI 14.4 to 15.7). The number of admitted patients with an ED LOS of ≥12 h increased by 13.8% (95% CI 10.3 to 17.3), while ED LOS among admitted patients increased from 13 h 17 min to 19 h 21 min (+29.0%; 95% CI 27.3 to 30.8). ED LOS increased most for admissions to medical wards but decreased for critical care admissions. Conclusions: In 2024, ED volumes were lower than in 2019, whereas ED occupancy, LWBS, and ED LOS were higher, with substantial heterogeneity across centers. These findings suggest a role for hospital output constraints, but the descriptive design does not establish causality.

articles.title: Intravesical Allogeneic Platelet Concentrate for Refractory BK Virus-Associated Haemorrhagic Cystitis After Allogeneic Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: BK virus-associated haemorrhagic cystitis (BKV-HC) is a severe complication of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) for which no standard treatment exists. Intravesical platelet-rich plasma has been proposed, but recipients are profoundly thrombocytopenic, and an autologous product cannot be obtained. We report the outcome of an intravesical allogeneic platelet concentrate (allo-PC) prepared from irradiated single-donor apheresis platelets in patients refractory to all available treatment. Methods: Single-centre retrospective series of 14 consecutive patients with Grade 3-4 BKV-HC treated between January 2018 and June 2021, selected from 84 patients who developed haemorrhagic cystitis during this period. All had failed hyperhydration, forced diuresis, continuous bladder irrigation and cidofovir; 10 had undergone previous cystoscopic cauterisation, 10 had immunosuppression reduction, and 4 had hyperbaric oxygen, all without resolution. The median duration of haematuria before allo-PC was 45.5 days. The primary outcome was resolution of macroscopic haematuria; transfusion requirement, catheter removal and readmission were reported separately. Results: Macroscopic haematuria resolved in 12 of 14 patients (85.7%, 95% CI 60.1-96.0) after a median of 5.5 days (IQR 4.0-12.5). Seven patients (50.0%, 95% CI 26.8-73.2) met all secondary criteria. Product platelet concentration correlated inversely with time to resolution (rs = -0.917, 95% CI -0.977 to -0.725). Because a fixed 50 mL volume was given, the delivered dose varied 18-fold (0.30-5.62 × 109 platelets/kg). Body weight also correlated with time to resolution (rs = +0.791), but in partial correlation the association with platelet concentration persisted after adjustment for weight (rs = -0.783, p = 0.004) and for age (rs = -0.827, p = 0.002), whereas the association with weight did not persist after adjustment for platelet concentration (rs = +0.292, p = 0.38). No procedure-related complication exceeded Clavien-Dindo Grade I. Conclusions: In patients who had exhausted all available treatment, intravesical allo-PC was followed by resolution of haematuria in most cases. The association between product platelet content and time to resolution was not explained by body weight or age. These uncontrolled findings are hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Emergency Medical Call-Taking and Dispatch Operations: A Scoping Review.

abstract.text: Objective: This study aimed to systematically review worldwide research on artificial intelligence (AI) applications in emergency medical service (EMS) call-taking and dispatch operations and identify current research trends and research needs. Methods: This scoping review was reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, KoreaMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library were searched for studies published from January 2021 to August 2026. Data were synthesized descriptively. Results: Eighteen studies from 13 countries and one multinational setting were included; eight (44.4%) were conducted in Europe. Patient Recognition and Classification was the predominant domain (11/18, 61.1%), followed by Dispatch Support and Operational Decision-Making (5/18, 27.8%) and Other Methodological Applications (2/18, 11.1%). Structured clinical or dispatch data were used in 11 studies, textual data in eight, and call audio in five; four applied multimodal integration. Deep learning (DL) was used as a primary model in 11 studies and classical machine learning (ML) in eight, including three using both; large language models (LLMs) were used in two. Eleven studies involved retrospective model development and internal validation, whereas only two were randomized controlled trials. None of the 11 model-development studies conducted independent external validation or calibration assessment, and the two randomized trials, one with high risk of bias and the other with some concerns, showed no consistent improvement across dispatch outcomes. Conclusions: AI applications span diverse clinical and operational tasks, with multimodal integration, speech technologies, and LLMs broadening their potential scope. Evidence remains dominated by retrospective model development and internal validation; prospective and real-world implementation studies are needed to establish safety and clinical utility before integration into EMS systems.

articles.title: Intra-arrest strategies to treat cardiac arrest due to a non-opioid toxicological causes in adults and children: a systematic review.
authors: Advanced Life Support and Pediatric Life Support Task Forces of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To summarise evidence on the effectiveness of specific alterations to standard advanced life support during ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults and children with cardiac arrest due to a presumed toxicological cause.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We searched MEDLINE (OVID platform), Embase (OVID platform), and Cochrane CENTRAL from inception to 22nd July 2026 for relevant observational and interventional studies with a control group. We excluded studies focussed specifically on opioid toxicity. Two authors independently screened studies for inclusion. Our primary outcome was 30-day survival. We assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane recommended tools and certainty of evidence using the GRADE system.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We identified four observational studies, of which none specifically focused on children and three included fewer than 100 patients. Studies examined general toxicological causes (n = 2), smoke inhalation and cyanide poisoning (n = 1), and beta-blocker and calcium-channel blocker overdose (n = 1). All studies were at critical risk of bias.Across the four studies, nine interventions were reported. Whilst some interventions were associated with either benefit or harm, estimates of effect were very imprecise and challenging to interpret. The largest study (1545 patients) reported that sodium bicarbonate use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to suspected drug overdose was associated with lower survival to hospital discharge (adjusted odds ratio 0.16, 95% confidence interval 0.08-0.31).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Current evidence does not support the modification of standard advanced life support during cardiac arrest due to a presumed toxicological cause in adults or children.Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251149412.

articles.title: Birthday Blues: Clinical Patterns of Emergency Department Visits Surrounding Birthdays.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Smaller studies have suggested that patients are more likely to present to the emergency department around the time of their birthdays. However, no multi-year analysis has been performed within the U.S. to uncover a possible association between birthdays and presentation to the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The objective of this study was to evaluate the overall frequency year after year of visits to the Emergency Department and the medical conditions most frequently encountered around the time of a birthday.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We studied emergency department visits from May 2018 to May 2024 at a Level 1 Trauma Center in a metropolitan city in the U.S.. Our analysis assessed the interval before or after ED presentation with respect to a patient's birthday. We utilized timeframes of ± 7 days (7 d) of one's birthday, ± 14 days (14 d), and ± 30 days (30 d) for analysis. We then conducted a descriptive analysis comparing proportions, standardized ratios (SR), and obtaining predictive probabilities from a multivariate logistic regression model.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 310,047 unique ED visits from 2018 to 2024, 12,650 visits were within ±7d of a patient's birthday. There were a greater than expected number of presentations ±7 d for all genders and age groups (particularly those <18 years old), and for those identifying as Asians. When looking at the role of chief complaint, individuals with a chief complaint related to Psychiatric/Toxicology, Trauma, Dermatologic, and Musculoskeletal concerns had a higher incidence of ED presentation ±7 d.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Across all populations, birthdays appear to be associated with an elevated risk of serious illness.

articles.title: Foreign body ingestion: how common is it really? A review and our experience managing a young woman: a case report.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Whether foreign body ingestion is the bigger problem or the underlying condition which prompts such behavior. Nowadays, published cases are evident enough to indicate the increasing frequency of foreign body ingestion reporting in the emergency department, particularly patients with psychiatric illnesses. Diagnosis is often prompted by complications such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and weight loss. The details of most recently published cases and their management are discussed in this article to have an idea that how commonly this condition is encountered in medical practice.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: This report presents a case of a 22-year-old Indian origin Muslim female, presented in our hospital with pain abdomen, nausea and vomiting just after taking meals. The patient's attendant mentioned that the ingestion was motivated by anger and a desire for attention from her parents and husband. An X-ray of the erect abdomen performed 8 days prior revealed heavy metal ingestion, and a computed tomography (CT) scan conducted 1 day before admission confirmed the presence of multiple foreign bodies in the stomach. On the day of surgery, a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) abdomen localized the cluster of foreign bodies in the second part of the duodenum. Initial attempts to remove the objects endoscopically were unsuccessful, necessitating surgical intervention after endoscopic retrieval failed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The incidence of foreign body ingestion seems to be increasing, with most cases managed endoscopically. However, in this case, the size and weight of the ingested objects, along with their clustering due to presence of magnets, made endoscopic retrieval challenging. This case highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing complex foreign body ingestions.

articles.title: Anti-Glioma Agents and Hyperbaric Oxygen for Prospective Therapeutic Approaches.

abstract.text: Adjuvant treatments for IDH-wild-type adult high-grade gliomas (HGGs) are being explored to improve therapeutic efficacy. Tumor hypoxia poses a major therapeutic challenge. In this narrative review, we discuss the potential of hyperbaric oxygen to counteract hypoxia and therapeutic resistance in HGG, with particular emphasis on glioblastoma. We delineate the pros and cons of combining treatment with hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) with established and experimental treatments for glioblastoma. HBO has been investigated as an adjuvant treatment alongside radiotherapy and chemotherapy, including new investigational compounds and approaches, with predominantly favorable outcomes in overall treatment efficacy. Among the numerous anticancer phytopharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals in this treatment paradigm, research on curcumin and its derivatives may lay the groundwork for promising future research directions and new chemical syntheses. The growing body of laboratory and clinical data suggests that HBO should be considered a promising component of modern oncological strategies for patients with HGG. However, further studies are needed to substantiate the effects of HBO since it has also been associated with increased tumor proliferation in some studies. Moreover, further studies are needed to substantiate the effects of HBO on tumor/immune interactions, stemness, therapy resistance, and patients' quality of life.

articles.title: Signs of Life and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The prognostic value of individual signs of life (SOLs) remains unclear in patients experiencing traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (t-OHCA).

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To describe clinical outcomes among patients with t-OHCA by the presence of each SOL at the scene.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data from the SOS-KANTO 2017 study, a multicenter prospective registry of OHCA cases treated between 2019 and 2021, were retrospectively analyzed. Adult patients diagnosed with t-OHCA were included, excluding those with a palpable pulse upon emergency medical service (EMS) arrival. Patients were categorized into eight subgroups based on the presence of three SOLs at the scene-the pupillary light reflex, spontaneous respiration, and cardiac electrical activity - and descriptive analyses were performed. The primary outcome was survival beyond the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 462 patients included in the analysis, two (0.4%) exhibited all three SOLs, and 18 (3.9%) exhibited two SOLs; in the latter group, two demonstrated cardiac activity and a pupillary reflex, and 16 had cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration. Among the 124 patients (26.8%) with only one SOL, 117 had cardiac activity, three showed a pupillary reflex, and four exhibited spontaneous respiration. No SOLs were observed in 318 patients (68.8%). Overall, 22 patients (4.8%) survived beyond the ED. The highest survival rate was observed in the subgroup with both cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration (4/16; 25%), followed by the subgroup with cardiac activity alone (10/117; 8.5%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among the t-OHCA patients, survival beyond the ED was observed more frequently in those with cardiac electrical activity at the scene.

articles.title: Efficacy of Inhaled Methoxyflurane for Acute Trauma Pain Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute traumatic pain is common in emergency settings and inadequate analgesia can worsen physiological, psychological, and functional outcomes.

abstract.label: STUDY OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy, onset of action, safety, and clinical practicality of inhaled methoxyflurane compared with control analgesic treatments for acute trauma-related pain.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Four databases were searched from inception through February 2026. Randomized controlled trials evaluating inhaled methoxyflurane for acute traumatic pain were eligible. Outcomes included visual analogue scale and numerical rating scale pain scores, rescue analgesia, time to first pain relief, and adverse events (AEs). Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and RevMan was used for quantitative synthesis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seven studies involving 1585 participants were analyzed. Methoxyflurane significantly reduced the time to first pain relief compared with controls (mean difference -5.93 min, 95% confidence interval [CI] -6.86 to -5.00, p < 0.00001, I2 = 0%). Pain intensity also favored methoxyflurane at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min. Methoxyflurane also significantly reduced the need for rescue analgesia (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.90, p = 0.03). Overall AEs were comparable, but dizziness, drowsiness, and cough were more frequent with methoxyflurane.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Inhaled methoxyflurane provides rapid and effective analgesia for acute traumatic pain and may reduce rescue analgesia needs. Further high-quality randomized trials are needed to clarify comparative effectiveness across trauma populations and emergency care settings.

articles.title: Interdisciplinary intervention (GAIN) vs. enhanced usual care for reducing severe post-concussion symptoms in adults 2-4 months post-injury: a stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Up to 30% of adults presenting to emergency departments develop persisting post-concussion symptoms (PPCS). Get going After concussIoN (GAIN), has previously shown promising effects in reducing PPCS in adolescents and young adults.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This stepped wedge cluster randomised trial tested the effect of GAIN in reducing high levels of PPCS (i.e. a score ≥20 on the Rivermead Post-concussion Symptoms Questionnaire (RPQ)) 2-4 months post-injury in adults (18-60 years). GAIN was delivered in five clusters of municipalities in the Central Denmark Region sequentially allocated to implement the intervention, with one cluster transitioning to deliver GAIN every 3 months over six recruitment periods in the order of a computer-generated randomisation schedule. Participants were allocated to enhanced usual care (EUC) or GAIN + EUC depending on time and their place of residence. Masking of participants and therapists was not feasible. Primary outcome was change in RPQ total score from baseline to 3-month follow-up. Analyses were based on intention to treat using linear-mixed models. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04798885.

abstract.label: FINDINGS
abstract.text: Between May 1, 2021 and November 1, 2022, 310 participants were included. The average difference in change in RPQ score between GAIN + EUC (n = 170) and EUC (n = 140) from baseline to 3-month follow-up was -2.4 points (95% CI -5.4 to 0.4, p = 0.09) in the adjusted model. GAIN reduced maladaptive, symptom-related perceptions and behaviours and patient satisfaction was high. GAIN + EUC was not associated with a greater improvement in psychological distress or physical and mental health than EUC. No serious adverse events were reported.

abstract.label: INTERPRETATION
abstract.text: This study could not confirm the hypothesis that GAIN added to EUC led to a larger long-term reduction in PPCS than EUC alone in adults. However, GAIN may improve long-term prognosis by reducing maladaptive, symptom-related perceptions and behaviours.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: The foundation Sygeforsikringen "danmark" and Central Denmark Region.

articles.title: Prognostic Impact of Transient Return of Spontaneous Circulation According to Low-Flow Time in Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Undergoing Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Nationwide Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Low-flow time (LFT) is a major prognostic factor in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), but chronological LFT may not fully reflect ischemic burden when transient return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) occurs. We investigated whether the association between transient ROSC and outcomes varies according to LFT. Methods: This nationwide retrospective cohort study included 810 adults with witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest who underwent ECPR. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge, and the secondary outcome was good neurological outcome. A prespecified subgroup analysis compared LFT ≤90 versus >90 min, followed by an exploratory analysis using <60, 60-90, and >90 min categories. Multivariable logistic regression and interaction analyses were performed. Results: Among 810 patients, 450 (55.6%) experienced transient ROSC. In the prespecified analysis, transient ROSC was associated with survival in patients with LFT ≤90 min (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 2.375; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.076-5.241; p = 0.032), but not in those with LFT >90 min (AOR, 0.884; 95% CI, 0.595-1.315; p = 0.543), with a significant interaction (p = 0.036). The exploratory three-category analysis showed a significant association in the 60-90-min subgroup (AOR, 3.399; 95% CI, 1.021-11.316; p = 0.046), although the global interaction was not significant (p = 0.126). No significant interaction was observed for good neurological outcome. The prespecified survival interaction remained significant in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: The association between transient ROSC and survival after ECPR differed according to LFT using the prespecified 90-min cutoff. Transient ROSC may provide prognostic information complementary to chronological LFT, whereas the three-category findings should be considered exploratory.

articles.title: Clinical accuracy and reliability of point-of-care ultrasound for perioperative diaphragmatic assessment: a scoping review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Diaphragmatic dysfunction contributes to perioperative respiratory morbidity. Point-of-care ultrasound enables noninvasive bedside assessment of diaphragmatic structure and motion and is increasingly used in perioperative practice. However, its diagnostic performance and measurement reliability in this setting have not been systematically evaluated. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence, with emphasis on reliability, reproducibility, and agreement with reference standards.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported as per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews. A protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. MEDLINE, MEDLINE ePubs and In-Process Citations, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases were searched. Eligible studies included adult or paediatric surgical patients undergoing perioperative diaphragmatic ultrasound. Data were charted on study characteristics, ultrasound techniques, reference standards, and measures of diagnostic accuracy and inter- and intra-observer agreement.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Nineteen studies (712 patients) were included, most being prospective observational and published after 2015. In adults, diaphragmatic ultrasound showed generally positive, although variable, correlations with spirometry, transdiaphragmatic pressure, electrophysiological measures, neuromuscular recovery, and arterial blood gas-based weaning criteria. Thresholds for excursion and thickening varied across studies. Inter- and intra-observer agreement was generally good to excellent, including among operators with limited training. In paediatric populations, ultrasound demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and strong agreement with fluoroscopy, with excellent interobserver reliability.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Perioperative diaphragmatic ultrasound shows acceptable reliability and agreement with reference standards. Heterogeneity in techniques and outcomes limits comparability. Standardisation and outcome-linked studies are needed to define its role.

articles.title: Pediatric Cholecystectomy: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Reduce Delays and Imaging Utilization.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Delays in surgical management of pediatric gallstone disease remain common. This quality improvement initiative evaluated contributors to delayed surgical management and implemented a standardized care protocol to improve hospital length of stay (LOS), time to cholecystectomy (TTC), and imaging utilization.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a two-phase quality improvement initiative at two pediatric hospitals within the same health system. Phase 1 was a retrospective cohort study of children ≤18 y old who underwent semiurgent cholecystectomy during admission for symptomatic cholelithiasis. Associations between hospital LOS and TTC and patient, clinical, and system-level factors were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression. Phase 1 findings informed a standardized algorithm, emphasizing early surgical consultation and risk stratification for choledocholithiasis. Phase 2 compared LOS, TTC, and preoperative magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) utilization before and after implementation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 187 preimplementation patients, 45% presented to the emergency department (ED) and 55% were transferred. Surgical consultation at presentation occurred in 74% of ED and 27% of transfers. Multivariable analysis demonstrated lower odds of LOS >2 d (odds ratio: 0.29, 95% confidence interval: 0.13-0.66) and TTC >2 d (odds ratio: 0.31, 95% confidence interval: 0.14-0.69) with early surgical consultation, independent of diagnosis, and point of entry. Following protocol implementation, median LOS decreased from 3 to 2 d and median TTC from 2 to 1 d (P < 0.001). MRCP utilization decreased from 39% to 24% (P = 0.013).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Implementation of a standardized, surgery-directed care pathway was associated with reduction in LOS, TTC, and MRCP utilization, supporting broader implementation and further refinement of pediatric choledocholithiasis risk stratification strategies.

articles.title: Cardiogenic Shock Systems of Care Best Practices. Part 1: Prehospital and Emergency Department Evaluation and Management.

abstract.text: This paper explores best practices for the prehospital and emergency department evaluation and management of cardiogenic shock, a critical condition marked by high mortality rates, within a contemporary cardiogenic shock system of care. It highlights the significance of early identification and immediate intervention to prevent irreversible cardiac and non-cardiac organ damage. Emphasizing multidisciplinary team-based care and data-driven insights, the paper details optimal strategies for managing cardiogenic shock from initial contact, noting challenges in prehospital identification and treatment due to patient and disease heterogeneity and the variability in response capabilities of prehospital teams.

articles.title: Feasibility and placement accuracy of a sensor-guided intraosseous device with an automated stop in a small-bone rat cadaver model: a single-arm pilot study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Rapid intraosseous (IO) access is critical in emergency care when venous access is not feasible. IO access is particularly prone to error in small animals and human neonates with narrow medullary cavities. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and placement accuracy of a novel sensor-guided IO drilling device with an automatic stop mechanism in a rat cadaver model.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Seven thawed Sprague-Dawley rat cadavers underwent 14 tibial insertions by a single experienced operator using a standardised protocol. Placement was assessed by computed tomography (CT), with successful insertion defined as intramedullary positioning of the needle tip. Two blinded readers independently classified each insertion. The principal outcome was the proportion of successful placements; a prespecified device-evaluable analysis excluding user-related targeting errors was exploratory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Nine of 14 insertions were correctly positioned, yielding a success rate of 64.3% (9/14; 95% CI 35.1-87.2%). In the device-evaluable analysis, success was 81.8% (9/11; 95% CI 48.2-97.7%). Three lateral displacements and two overpenetrations occurred. Reader agreement was complete (κ = 1.00). The medullary cavity narrowed from 6.02 mm at the proximal metaphysis to 3.13 mm at the diaphysis, with cortical thickness of 0.54-0.57 mm; proximal epiphyseal outer diameter of 8.07 mm. No device malfunction was identified.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this small-bone cadaver model, the automated-stop intraosseous device achieved CT-verified intramedullary placement in most attempts and functioned as intended. As this single-arm pilot lacked a comparator and CT assessed needle-tip position rather than functional access, the findings are limited to placement accuracy and are hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Improving Arterial Blood Gas Sampling Practice in the Emergency Department: A Two-Cycle Clinical Audit.

abstract.text: Background Arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling is commonly performed in emergency care but is invasive and painful, particularly when repeated sampling is required. In selected patients with acute respiratory disease, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, venous blood gas (VBG) analysis can provide useful screening information and may avoid unnecessary arterial puncture. A venous PCO₂ below 6.0 kPa, when interpreted alongside satisfactory pulse oximetry and the clinical context, can help exclude significant arterial hypercapnia, while venous pH is generally sufficiently close to arterial pH for initial assessment. Despite this, clinicians may still default to arterial sampling, and measures intended to reduce procedural pain, such as local anaesthesia, are not always routinely used. We evaluated whether a targeted educational intervention could improve clinicians' knowledge and reported practice relating to ABG sampling. Methods We conducted a two-cycle clinical audit in a UK emergency department. Cycle 1 included 59 clinicians and identified baseline gaps in VBG knowledge, local anaesthetic use and patient-centred sampling practice. A multimodal intervention was subsequently introduced, combining departmental teaching, a short educational video, visual prompts and reinforcement during clinical work. Cycle 2 included 30 clinicians. Prespecified measures assessed knowledge of when VBG may provide adequate initial information, routine skin antisepsis and local anaesthetic use. Ultrasound use for difficult arterial access and enquiry about patient pain or experience were also assessed. As responses were anonymous and could not be paired between cycles, the two samples were analysed independently. Results Mean VBG knowledge increased from 51.7% (n/N = 61/118) in Cycle 1 to 75.0% (n/N = 45/60) in Cycle 2, an absolute improvement of 23.3 percentage points (95% CI 7.2-39.4; p = 0.005; Hedges g = 0.61). The proportion of clinicians answering both VBG knowledge items correctly increased from 32.2% (n/N = 19/59) to 60.0% (n/N = 18/30). Recognition that a normal venous pH and PCO₂ does not automatically require arterial confirmation increased from 67.8% (n/N = 40/59) to 90.0% (n/N = 27/30), while recognition of the potential role of VBG with pulse oximetry increased from 35.6% (n/N = 21/59) to 60.0% (n/N = 18/30). Local anaesthetic use increased from 6.8% (n/N = 4/59) to 23.3% (n/N = 7/30) (absolute difference 16.6 percentage points; 95% CI 1.7-34.6; p = 0.039), although it remained the largest gap from the prespecified standard. Routine skin antisepsis remained consistently high at 96.6% (n/N = 57/59) versus 96.7% (n/N = 29/30). Enquiry about patient pain or experience increased from 50.8% (n/N = 30/59) to 80.0% (n/N = 24/30) (difference 29.2 percentage points; 95% CI 7.9-45.4; p = 0.011). Ultrasound use for difficult arterial access increased from 47.5% (n/N = 28/59) to 66.7% (n/N = 20/30). Conclusions After the multimodal intervention, VBG knowledge and several aspects of reported ABG practice improved. Local anaesthetic use remained low despite some improvement, suggesting that education alone may not be enough to change this procedural behaviour. Appropriate use of VBG in selected patients, together with better analgesia when ABG sampling is required, may reduce unnecessary arterial puncture and procedural pain. Future cycles should directly measure ABG indications, procedural practice and patient-reported pain.

articles.title: Unilateral Headache as a Presentation of Spontaneous Internal Carotid Artery Dissection: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Spontaneous internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection is a rare but potentially serious cause of ischemic stroke, with a frequently heterogeneous clinical presentation that poses a diagnostic challenge, particularly in primary care settings. We report a case of a 46-year-old female with a history of migraine, resolved thyrotoxicosis, and oral contraceptive use, who presented to her family health unit with a 15-day history of left-sided hemicranial headache preceded by ipsilateral neck pain without identifiable trauma. Associated findings included left ptosis, ipsilateral scalp hyperesthesia, and taste disturbance affecting the posterior third of the tongue, in the absence of motor deficits, aphasia, or visual changes. She was referred to the emergency department, where CT angiography revealed narrowing of the left ICA at the post-bulbar segment, raising suspicion of dissection, subsequently confirmed by cervical Doppler ultrasound and magnetic resonance angiography, which demonstrated a minimally opacified false lumen with mild-to-moderate stenosis and no cerebral ischemia. An extended etiological workup was negative. Dual antiplatelet therapy was initiated, and the patient achieved complete neurological recovery, being discharged on hospital day 7. Follow-up imaging identified the development of a pseudoaneurysm at the post-bulbar segment of the left ICA without hemodynamic significance. The patient remains under neurology and family medicine follow-up with persistent headache and cervicalgia under pharmacological management. This case highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of clinical suspicion in primary care when faced with persistent unilateral headache associated with cranial nerve signs, even in the absence of overt stroke, and underscores the role of the general practitioner in the early recognition of warning signs, timely referral, and continuity of care.

articles.title: A Case of Acute Spontaneous Spinal Epidural Hematoma Caused by Repeated Bleeding Thoracic Radiculomeningeal Artery.

abstract.text: Spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma (SSEH) presents with back pain followed by myelopathy. Venous plexus disruption is common, and arterial bleeding is extremely rare. Here, we report a case of acute spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma that showed spot sign on computed tomographic angiography and was treated. A 48-year-old woman with no medical history experienced unprovoked back pain and visited a local hospital, where she was placed under observation. Numbness gradually developed in both legs, and the patient visited our emergency room 5 hours after the onset of symptoms. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma on the left ventrolateral side at the T4-6 level, and computed tomographic angiography showed a spot sign at T5-6. During the examination, the patient's paraplegia progressed, and she presented with bladder-rectum dysfunction. She was diagnosed with spinal shock and underwent emergency surgery 9 hours after the onset of symptoms. The hematoma was removed and the source of arterial bleeding was treated, generating a complete recovery. In cases of acutely progressing paraplegic spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma, contrast-enhanced computed tomographic angiography is useful for identifying the source of bleeding, and in cases of arterial bleeding, emergency decompression and vascular ligation are useful.

articles.title: Clinical practice guidelines: management of non-post-operative supra-ventricular tachycardia in neonates and children less than 18 years old hospitalized in a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit.
authors: French Speaking Group for Pediatric Intensive and Emergency Care

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: We present guidelines in the form of pragmatic recommendations for management of neonates and children less than 18 years old presenting with non-post-operative supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) and hospitalized in a Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Thirteen French-speaking experts, all of them members of the Groupe Francophone de Réanimation et Urgence Pédiatriques (French-speaking group of paediatric intensive and emergency care; GFRUP), collaborated from 2024 to 2025 through teleconferences and face-to-face meetings. The guidelines cover four areas: (1) epidemiology and criteria for admission to a PICU, (2) paraclinical assessment, (3) non-specific rhythm management, and (4) specific rhythm management. The questions were formulated in the Patient-Intervention-Comparison-Outcome (PICO) format. An extensive Anglophone and Francophone literature search indexed in the MEDLINE database via PubMed, Cochrane and Embase was performed using pre-established keywords. The texts were analyzed and classified according to the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. When this method was not applicable, an expert opinion was given. Each of the recommendations was voted on by all the experts according to the Delphi methodology.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The group proposes 21 recommendations. The GRADE methodology could be applied for five of them, and an expert opinion was given for the remaining 16. All of the recommendations received strong approval.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These guidelines cover different aspects in the management of non-post-operative SVT in children hospitalized in PICUs including non-specific and specific rhythm management.

articles.title: A Comparative Outcomes Study: Is Routine Hip Abduction Bracing Necessary After Gluteus Medius Repair?

abstract.text: Introduction Postoperative protocols regarding hip bracing after the surgical repair of a gluteus medius tear remain variable. It is unclear whether hip bracing improves short-term outcomes in patients undergoing gluteus medius repair. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the combined six-month complication and reoperation rate before and after discontinuing postoperative hip brace use after a gluteus medius repair. Methods A retrospective review of 162 patients undergoing gluteus medius repair by a single, fellowship-trained surgeon was performed. The no-brace protocol was implemented in October 2020. Prior to October 2020, all patients were prescribed a postoperative brace, and this served as the historical control group. Starting in October 2020, the postoperative brace was no longer prescribed, and this served as the study group. The remainder of the perioperative protocol was the same for both groups. All patients immediately began physical therapy and had toe-touch weightbearing restrictions for three weeks postoperatively. The primary endpoint was the combined complication and reoperation rate within six months postoperatively. Results The groups were similar demographically, with the only significant difference being that the no-brace group had a higher percentage of patients undergo open repair (29 (33.7%) vs. 14 (18.4%); p=0.028). There were no significant differences in outcomes at 30 days when looking at emergency department returns (2 (2.3%) vs. 4 (5.3%); p=0.421) and readmissions (0% vs. 2 (2.6%); p=0.219). At six weeks, there were no significant differences in falls (2 (2.3%) vs. 1 (1.3%); p=1.000) and other complications (1 (1.2%) vs. 2 (2.6%); p=0.601). Similarly, at six months, there were no significant differences in falls (4 (4.7%) vs. 1 (1.3%); p=0.372) and other complications including deep vein thrombosis, re-tear, fibromyalgia flare, and fracture (5 (5.8%) vs. 5 (6.6%); p=0.840). There was also no significant difference between groups in reoperation rates within six months (0% vs. 2 (2.6%); p=0.219). The combined six-month complication and reoperation rate was also not significant between groups (10 (11.6%) vs. 9 (11.8%); p=0.966). Conclusion In patients undergoing gluteus medius repair, postoperative bracing was not associated with differences in complication rates over the six-month postoperative period. Based on this result, discontinuation of postoperative bracing appears safe in this population. Further study is needed to replicate these results with a larger sample size.

articles.title: Manual ventilation with and without a flow limiting device during induction of general anesthesia: a randomized crossover trial.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE
abstract.text: Poor manual ventilation with a self-inflating resuscitator bag (SIRB) can result in excessive tidal volumes and elevated airway pressures, increasing the risk of gastric insufflation, aspiration and lung injury. This study compared peak airway pressures generated during intentionally forceful manual ventilation using a SIRB with, and without a flow-limiting device in patients undergoing non-emergent surgery.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this randomized, two-group crossover superiority trial, 30 adult patients undergoing general anesthesia received manual SIRB ventilation with and without the Sotair® inline flow limiting device (FLD) in randomized order (FLD + SIRB followed by SIRB alone vs SIRB alone followed by FLD + SIRB). Following endotracheal intubation, the SIRB, FLD, flow and pressure sensor, and adjustable pressure-limiting valve were connected in series to the endotracheal tube. During each intervention period, five forceful breaths were delivered every 30 s for 3 min. For safety, a pressure-limiting valve was set at 35 cm H2O. The primary outcome was the mean peak inspiratory pressure across the five forceful breaths.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The mean peak inspiratory pressure across five forceful breaths was 18.4 cm H2O [95% CI, 17.2-19.6] with FLD + SIRB compared to 29.6 cm H2O [95% CI, 28.4-30.8] with SIRB ventilation alone, with a mean difference of 11.2 cm H2O [95% CI, 10.5-11.9], which was above the superiority margin of 7.5 cm H2O (p < 0.001). Mean peak inspiratory flow (60.1 L/min [95% CI, 55.7-64.6] vs 101.7 L/min [95% CI, 97.2-106.1]) and tidal volume (96.7 mL [95% CI, 77.6-115.9] vs 789.2 mL [95% CI, 770.1-808.3]) were also significantly lower with the FLD + SIRB compared to SIRB alone (p < 0.001). No FLD related malfunction events were observed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The novel flow-limiting device reduced excessive peak airway pressures, inspiratory flow, and tidal volumes during forceful SIRB ventilation in anesthetized, intubated adults undergoing elective surgery. However, reduced tidal volumes during forceful breaths may cause inadequate alveolar ventilation if not corrected over several breaths, particularly during CPR.

articles.title: Sociodemographic and Clinical Profile of Homeless Patients Attending the Emergency Department of a Tertiary Care Centre in Rishikesh, Uttarakhand, India: A Prospective Observational Study.

abstract.text: Introduction Homeless individuals are a highly vulnerable population with complex medical and social needs. Emergency departments (EDs) often serve as the primary point of contact for healthcare for homeless persons in India, yet systematic data on their profile and outcomes from tertiary care settings remain limited. Methodology A prospective observational study was conducted in the emergency medicine department of a tertiary care centre in North India from July 2022 to December 2023 (18-month duration). All homeless patients aged over 18 years presenting to the emergency department and meeting inclusion criteria were enrolled. Sociodemographic data, clinical presentation, investigations, consultations and ED outcomes were recorded using a structured pro forma, and data were analysed using SPSS v23.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Results Forty-eight homeless patients were enrolled in the study. The majority were men (93.8%), adults aged 31-60 years (52.1%) and from Uttarakhand (85.4%). Most patients (75%) were staying alone, and 81.2% were uninsured. The most common mode of arrival was ambulance (85.4%), with 66.7% referred from another healthcare facility. The most common presenting complaints were abdominal symptoms (22.9%), dyspnoea (18.8%) and trauma (16.7%). Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was the most common diagnosis (12.5%), followed by head injury (10.4%) and decompensated chronic liver disease (8.3%). Two-thirds of the patients (66.7%) were triaged to the red area. ED in-hospital mortality was 18.8%. The median ED length of stay was two days. Fourteen patients had ED revisits during the study period. Conclusions Homeless patients presenting to the ED are predominantly men and uninsured and arrive in critical condition via ambulance. They carry a high burden of chronic disease, present late in the course of illness and have substantially high in-ED mortality. Integrated care models, policy-level expansion of health coverage and dedicated ED protocols for homeless individuals are urgently needed in India.

articles.title: Emergency Department Management of Ankle Fractures: A Narrative Review.

abstract.text: Ankle fractures are among the most common orthopedic injuries encountered in the emergency department. Nearly half occur secondary to low-energy mechanisms such as ground-level falls, and approximately one-fourth ultimately require surgery. Appropriate acute management and disposition by providers in the acute setting is crucial to optimizing patient outcomes. This begins with a general knowledge of the commonly used Danis-Weber and Lauge-Hansen classification system, which helps categorize the majority of ankle fracture patterns encountered. Initial management includes timely reduction, multimodal pain control, and appropriate immobilization. Available resources, provider experience, and interfacility practice patterns influence specific management decisions; however, multiple effective treatment strategies exist. This review provides a concise resource regarding emergency department management and the different reduction maneuvers that can be utilized.

articles.title: Tricuspid Valve Infective Endocarditis Seen on Point-of-Care Ultrasound: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Intravenous drug use is a major risk factor for infective endocarditis (IE), particularly right-sided disease involving the tricuspid valve. Early diagnosis remains challenging as patients often present with nonspecific symptoms, while delays in recognition can result in severe complications including septic emboli, valvular dysfunction, and sepsis. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has emerged as a valuable bedside modality capable of rapidly identifying valvular abnormalities and expediting the diagnosis of IE in the emergency department. We present a case of tricuspid valve infective endocarditis in a patient with a history of intravenous drug use in whom cardiac POCUS identified a large tricuspid vegetation prior to comprehensive echocardiography. Subsequent evaluation demonstrated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia with multiple septic embolic complications. The patient ultimately underwent percutaneous vegetation debulking in addition to intravenous antibiotic therapy. This case highlights the utility of bedside cardiac POCUS in facilitating rapid recognition, expedited specialty consultation, and timely management of infective endocarditis in high-risk patients presenting to the emergency department.

articles.title: Beyond Primary Epilepsy: Fahr's Syndrome Secondary to Congenital Parathyroid Agenesis Presenting With Generalised Seizures in a Young Adult.

abstract.text: Symmetrical, bilateral intracranial calcifications, commonly involving the basal ganglia, constitute the characteristic features of Fahr's syndrome, which is an uncommon neurometabolic condition. Its incidence in conjunction with congenital parathyroid agenesis, however, has rarely been reported. The present case emphasises how crucial it is to identify the metabolic origins of intracranial calcification and differentiate Fahr's syndrome from primary familial brain calcification to prevent repeated neurological consequences through adequate therapy. A 26-year-old man with congenital absence of the parathyroid gland presented to the emergency department after a 10-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure, preceded by twitching of the perioral muscles. Examination revealed continuous perioral twitching, drowsiness in the postictal state and a positive Chvostek sign. Although the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OH vitamin D) level remained within the normal range (88 nmol/L), laboratory tests revealed severe hypocalcaemia (1.44 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (1.95 mmol/L) and undetectable parathyroid hormone (<0.1 pmol/L), supporting hypoparathyroidism as the underlying cause of his symptoms. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head demonstrated typical bilateral symmetric basal ganglia calcifications, consistent with Fahr's syndrome, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed QT interval prolongation. Intravenous calcium, oral calcium supplements, and alfacalcidol were used to treat the patient; this led to the correction of hypocalcaemia, full resolution of neuromuscular symptoms and no more seizures while the patient was in the hospital. This case demonstrates the rare correlation between Fahr's syndrome and congenital parathyroid agenesis that manifests in early adulthood. It highlights how crucial it is to take reversible metabolic factors into account when young adults exhibit new-onset seizures. Adequate vitamin D stores alone cannot maintain calcium homeostasis in individuals with congenital hypoparathyroidism, as evidenced by the significant hypocalcaemia that developed despite normal vitamin D status due to lacking parathyroid hormone.

articles.title: The Use of Situational Judgement Tests for Paramedic Selection in Canada: A National Cross-Sectional Survey.

abstract.text: Background It is important for paramedics to have strong interpersonal and cognitive skills. Despite the importance of such skills, the paramedic field has incorporated few tools to evaluate these attributes. Situational Judgment Tests (SJTs) are psychometric tools that use scenario-based questions to quantify personal and cognitive attributes. Though extensive literature exists on the use of SJTs, few studies explore the current state of SJT use in the paramedic field. Methods In this national survey study, we aimed to understand the current use of SJTs and other tools in the hiring of frontline paramedics by Canadian paramedic services. The survey also included questions about the use of Multiple Mini Interview (MMI), which are station-based interviews that have been found to validly evaluate the interpersonal and cognitive skills of paramedics for the purpose of hiring decisions. Results A total of 21 services left unique, complete responses. Neither SJTs nor MMIs are widely used in Canada. Only smaller paramedic services reported that they were using SJTs and MMIs, despite these tools being designed for mass testing. Conclusions Though a role has been identified for SJTs in paramedic selection and education, paramedic services in Canada do not appear to widely use SJTs to inform their hiring processes.

articles.title: Cardiac arrest as the first sign of thyrotoxicosis: a case report of angiographically proven coronary vasospasm.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Cardiovascular manifestations of thyrotoxicosis are common, typically presenting as tachyarrhythmias or high-output physiology. Coronary artery spasm (CAS) is an uncommon but increasingly recognized complication, usually causing transient ischaemia rather than malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Cardiac arrest due to thyrotoxicosis-induced CAS is exceedingly rare. Early recognition is vital because management differs from that of typical acute coronary syndromes (ACS).

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 63-year-old man suffered an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with an initial shockable rhythm, achieving return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after a single defibrillation. Initial evaluation revealed inferior ST-segment elevation, leading to urgent coronary angiography, which demonstrated severe right coronary artery spasm that resolved after intracoronary nitrate administration. Laboratory studies confirmed significant hyperthyroidism, and recurrent ST-segment changes in the intensive care unit further supported thyrotoxicosis-induced CAS as the underlying mechanism. The patient made a full neurological and cardiac recovery following temperature management, intensification of antithyroid therapy, and vasodilator treatment.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case underscored an unusual presentation of cardiac arrest triggered by thyrotoxicosis-related CAS in the absence of underlying coronary artery disease. Elevated thyroid hormone levels can impair endothelial function and heighten vascular smooth muscle reactivity, creating a predisposition to diffuse, therapy-resistant vasospasm.
